title: HTML — The Skeleton of Every Web Page
description: Learn the 10 HTML tags you'll use 90% of the time. Build a real page, not a toy.
learningObjectives: I can explain what HTML is and what it does
I can use the 10 most important HTML tags
I can build a basic web page with text, links, and images

contentSections.title: What HTML actually is

contentSections.body: Every website you've ever visited — from Google to your favorite blog — is built on HTML. It's been around since 1991 and it's not going anywhere. HTML is the skeleton. CSS is the skin. JavaScript is the muscles. Start with the skeleton.

**HTML** (HyperText Markup Language) describes the *structure* of a web page using tags. A tag looks like this: `content` Every HTML file has the same basic structure: ```html My Page

Hello, world!

``` - `` — metadata, page title, links to CSS (not visible) - `` — everything the user sees

contentSections.question: What's the difference between `<head>` and `<body>` in an HTML document?
contentSections.answer: `<head>` contains metadata about the page (title, CSS links, charset) — invisible to users. `<body>` contains the actual visible content — text, images, buttons, everything users see and interact with.
contentSections.hint: Think about what a user can see vs. what the browser reads but doesn't show

contentSections.body: HTML is structure, not design. You're telling the browser *what* things are (heading, paragraph, link), not how they look.

contentSections.title: The 10 tags you'll use every day

contentSections.body:
You don't need to memorize all HTML tags. These 10 cover 90% of real use: ```html

Main title

Section title

A paragraph of text.

Bold text Italic text Click here
  • Item 1
  • Item 2
A container for grouping elements
``` **Always include `alt` on images** — it's required for accessibility and SEO.

**Ask Claude to scaffold HTML for you.** 'Write an HTML page with a header, a main section with 3 feature cards, and a footer. Use semantic HTML.' Claude will generate the structure; you customize the content.

contentSections.question: Why does every `` tag need an `alt` attribute?
contentSections.answer: Screen readers (used by blind and low-vision users) read the alt text aloud. Search engines also use alt text to understand images. Missing alt = inaccessible page. Empty alt (`alt=""`) is valid for decorative images — it tells screen readers to skip it.
contentSections.hint: Think about users who can't see the image — how do they know what it shows?

contentSections.body: Learn 10 tags deeply, not 100 tags shallowly. h1-h2, p, a, img, ul/li, div, button — that's 90% of real HTML.

contentSections.title: Build your first page — right now

contentSections.scenario: ```html ```
contentSections.question: What's missing for accessibility and SEO?

options.label: Nothing — this is a complete, correct image tag
The alt attribute — a text description for screen readers

feedback.missing: Right — alt is required for accessibility and SEO. Without it, screen reader users get nothing describing the image.
feedback.fine: Not quite — src alone displays the image visually, but alt is required for accessibility and SEO.

contentSections.concept: Always include alt on images — it's required for accessibility and SEO. ``

contentSections.body:
Create a file called `index.html` and open it in your browser. Build a personal intro page: ```html Sarah Chen — Portfolio

Sarah Chen

Freelance designer learning to code from bed. Chronic illness warrior.

What I'm building

  • Design automation tools
  • Accessibility-first web apps

``` Open `index.html` in Chrome. You have a website. It's ugly — CSS comes next — but it *works*.

title: CSS — Make It Look Good
description: CSS turns your HTML skeleton into something beautiful. Colors, fonts, spacing, layout — all CSS.
learningObjectives: I can write CSS selectors to target HTML elements
I can apply colors, fonts, and spacing with CSS
I can use Flexbox to create simple layouts

contentSections.title: CSS selectors — targeting elements

contentSections.body: Right now your HTML page looks like a Word document from 1995. CSS is what makes it look like a real website. Same HTML content, completely different appearance — all controlled by CSS.

contentSections.question: Why should you use classes instead of IDs for most styling?
contentSections.answer: IDs must be unique per page — you can only use an ID once. Classes can be reused on multiple elements. If you have 6 cards, you use `class='card'` on all 6. `id='card'` would only work on one.
contentSections.hint: Think about what 'ID' means — can two people have the same ID?

contentSections.body: CSS selects elements and applies styles. Tag selectors are broad, class selectors are reusable, ID selectors are unique.

contentSections.title: Colors, fonts, and the box model

contentSections.question: You have a button with `padding: 12px 24px`. What does this mean?
contentSections.answer: 12px top and bottom (vertical), 24px left and right (horizontal). Shorthand: `padding: [top/bottom] [left/right]`. For all four sides: `padding: 12px 24px 12px 24px` (top right bottom left — clockwise).

contentSections.body: Padding = space inside the element. Margin = space outside. When layout looks wrong, check these first.

contentSections.title: Flexbox — modern layout in 5 properties

contentSections.scenario: Your card's content sits fine against its own border, but there's a big unwanted gap between the card and the elements around it.
contentSections.question: Which CSS property controls that outer gap?

options.label: padding
margin

feedback.margin: Right — margin is space outside the border, between this element and its neighbors.
feedback.padding: Not quite — padding is space inside the border, between the border and the content. The gap between elements is margin.

contentSections.concept: Padding = inside the border. Margin = outside the border. When things look wrong, it's usually a padding/margin issue.

title: JavaScript in the Browser — DOM Basics
description: Your JavaScript can change the page. Click a button, update the content. This is interactivity.
learningObjectives: I can select HTML elements with JavaScript
I can respond to user clicks with event listeners
I can update page content dynamically with JavaScript

contentSections.title: What the DOM is

contentSections.body:
When you write `

Hello

` in HTML, the browser turns it into a JavaScript object you can access and modify. Change the object, the page updates instantly. This is the DOM — and it's how every interactive website works.

contentSections.question: What's the difference between `querySelector` and `querySelectorAll`?
contentSections.answer: `querySelector` returns the *first* matching element (or null if none found). `querySelectorAll` returns *all* matching elements as a NodeList (like an array). Use `querySelector` when you want one element, `querySelectorAll` when you want to work with multiple.

contentSections.body: The DOM is your bridge between JavaScript and HTML. Select an element, change its properties, the page updates instantly.

contentSections.title: Event listeners — respond to users

contentSections.body: **Event listener gotcha:** Make sure the HTML element exists before you add a listener. If your JS runs before the HTML loads, `querySelector` returns `null` and `null.addEventListener()` throws an error. Wrap your code in `document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', () => { ... })` or put your `<script>` tag at the bottom of `<body>`.

contentSections.question: What does `event.target` refer to inside an event listener callback?
contentSections.answer: `event.target` is the specific element that triggered the event. For a click listener on a button, `event.target` is that button element. For an input listener, `event.target.value` gives you what the user typed.
contentSections.hint: Think about the arrow pointing at 'target' — what did the user actually interact with?

contentSections.body: `.addEventListener('event', callback)` is how your code listens for user actions. `event.target` is the element they interacted with.

contentSections.title: Build a counter — your first interactive app

contentSections.question: After the user clicks once, what happens if they click again?

options.label: The handler runs again — textContent updates, disabled toggles off
Nothing — the button is now disabled, so it can't be clicked

feedback.disabled: Right — button.disabled = true means the button can no longer be clicked until something re-enables it.
feedback.runs-again: Not quite — disabled = true blocks further clicks entirely; the handler won't fire again until disabled is set back to false somewhere else in the code.

contentSections.concept: button.disabled = true prevents further interaction with that element. Event listeners only fire on elements the user can actually interact with.

title: Forms & User Input
description: Get data from users. Forms, validation, and handling what users type — essential for any real app.
learningObjectives: I can build an HTML form and access its values with JavaScript
I can validate user input before processing it
I can prevent a form from reloading the page

contentSections.title: Building HTML forms

contentSections.body: Forms are everywhere: login pages, checkout flows, contact forms, settings pages. If a user needs to give you data, you need a form. Master forms and you can build the input layer for any app.

The core form elements:

```html
<form id="signup-form">
  <!-- Text input -->
  <label for="name">Your name</label>
  <input type="text" id="name" name="name" placeholder="Sarah" required>

  <!-- Email input -->
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>

  <!-- Password -->
  <input type="password" id="password" minlength="8">

  <!-- Checkbox -->
  <input type="checkbox" id="terms" name="terms">
  <label for="terms">I agree to the terms</label>

  <!-- Dropdown -->
  <select id="plan" name="plan">
    <option value="free">Free</option>
    <option value="pro">Pro — €12/month</option>
  </select>

  <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
</form>
```

**Always pair `<label>` with `<input>` using `for`/`id`** — required for accessibility.

contentSections.question: Why should you always pair `<label>` with `<input>`?
contentSections.answer: Screen readers announce the label when the input gets focus — without it, users don't know what the field is for. Also, clicking a label focuses the associated input, improving usability (especially for checkboxes which are hard to click precisely).
contentSections.hint: Think about screen readers and what happens when you click a label

contentSections.body: Always pair labels with inputs using for/id. Use `required`, `type`, and `minlength` for built-in HTML validation.

contentSections.title: Handling form submission with JavaScript

contentSections.question: What happens if you forget `event.preventDefault()` in your form submit handler?
contentSections.answer: The browser submits the form the old-fashioned way: the page reloads, query params appear in the URL (for GET forms), and your JavaScript state is lost. Your `console.log` will appear for a split second, then the page refreshes.
contentSections.hint: What does a form do by default when submitted?

contentSections.body: `event.preventDefault()` prevents page reload. Always call it first in form submit handlers.

contentSections.title: Client-side validation

contentSections.scenario: A form's submit handler runs validation but never calls event.preventDefault().
contentSections.question: What happens when the user submits a valid form?

options.label: Your validation runs, then the page reloads and you lose the JS state
Nothing — the browser waits for you to explicitly submit

feedback.reloads: Right — by default, submitting a form reloads the page. Without event.preventDefault(), your validation and any JS state you built get wiped the instant the user submits.
feedback.nothing: Not quite — the browser's default form behavior submits and reloads immediately; it doesn't wait for you to opt in, you have to opt out with preventDefault().

contentSections.concept: event.preventDefault() is the most important line in any form handler. Always start with it — otherwise submitting a form reloads the page and you lose all your data.

contentSections.body: **Client-side validation is UX, not security.** It's easily bypassed. Always validate again on the server. Never trust data coming from the browser.

title: Deploy to Vercel — 5 Minutes to Live
description: Get your app on the internet. Vercel makes deployment stupidly easy. Go from local file to live URL.
learningObjectives: I can push my project to GitHub
I can deploy a static site to Vercel in under 5 minutes
I can understand the difference between a local and a deployed app

contentSections.title: Why deployment matters

contentSections.body: An app on your laptop is just a file. An app on the internet is a product. The difference between a hobbyist and a developer is shipping. Today you ship.

**What deployment means:**

Right now, your `index.html` lives on your laptop. Only you can see it (by opening the file). Deployment means uploading it to a server that's always on, so *anyone with a URL* can see it.

**Three deployment layers:**
1. **Your code** → uploaded to GitHub (version control + source)
2. **Vercel** → reads your GitHub repo, hosts the files on their servers
3. **Users** → visit your Vercel URL, get your files served from a nearby server

**Vercel** is free for personal projects. It auto-deploys every time you push to GitHub. No server config required.

contentSections.question: Why is it better to deploy from GitHub instead of uploading files directly to a server?
contentSections.answer: GitHub keeps your history — you can roll back if something breaks. Vercel watches your GitHub repo and auto-deploys on every push, so you never manually upload files. It also lets collaborators contribute without server access.
contentSections.hint: Think about what happens when a deployment breaks — how do you recover?

contentSections.body: GitHub = source of truth. Vercel = automatic deployment from GitHub. Push to GitHub → live in 2 minutes.

contentSections.title: Git basics — the 3 commands you need

contentSections.body:
You don't need to master Git to deploy. Learn these 5 commands:

```bash
# 1. Initialize a Git repo in your project
git init

# 2. Stage all your files
git add .

# 3. Commit (save a snapshot)
git commit -m "Initial commit — personal portfolio page"

# 4. Connect to GitHub (after creating a repo on github.com)
git remote add origin https://github.com/yourusername/my-portfolio.git

# 5. Push to GitHub
git push -u origin main
```

You'll run `git add . && git commit -m 'description' && git push` every time you make changes you want to deploy.

If you get confused by git, ask Claude: 'I'm getting this git error: [paste error]. What does it mean?'

contentSections.question: What does `git commit -m 'Fix typo in nav'` do?
contentSections.answer: It saves a snapshot of your staged files with the message 'Fix typo in nav'. Like saving a checkpoint in a video game — you can return to any commit later. The `-m` flag lets you write the message inline.
contentSections.hint: Think of git commits as save points — what does this save point do?

contentSections.body: Git: add → commit → push. Three commands to version your code and push to GitHub.

contentSections.title: Deploy on Vercel — step by step

contentSections.question: Put these git commands in the order you'd run them for a brand-new project.
steps: git remote add origin <your GitHub repo URL>
contentSections.explanation: init creates the repo, add stages your files, commit saves a snapshot, remote add connects to the GitHub repo you created, and push sends it there. After this one-time setup, every future update is just add, commit, and push.

contentSections.body:
Once your code is on GitHub:

1. Go to **vercel.com** → Sign up with GitHub
2. Click **'Add New Project'**
3. Find your GitHub repo in the list → click **Import**
4. Vercel auto-detects your project type
5. Click **Deploy** — takes about 60 seconds
6. You get a URL like `my-portfolio-abc123.vercel.app`

**Your site is live.**

Every future `git push` to your main branch auto-deploys a new version.

**Custom domain (optional):**
- Buy a domain on Porkbun (~€10/year)
- In Vercel → Domains → Add `yourdomain.com`
- Add the DNS records Vercel tells you to
- Wait 5 minutes → `yourdomain.com` points to your app
**Vercel free tier covers:** Unlimited personal projects, 100GB bandwidth/month, automatic HTTPS, global CDN. You will not need to pay for hosting unless you're getting thousands of daily users.

title: A page is a document with structure
description: A web page isn't decorated text — it's a document made of nested elements, each one telling the browser (and anyone using a screen reader) what a piece of content actually is.

learningObjectives.text: Explain that an HTML element is an opening tag, content, and a closing tag
Identify a complete, correctly nested element versus a broken one
Build the standard html/head/body skeleton every page starts from

contentSections.title: Everything on the page is inside a tag

contentSections.body: You paste "Ibuprofen 400mg — 8am, 2pm, 8pm" into a plain text file and email it to whoever's picking up your prescription. It reads fine. Paste the exact same text into an HTML file and open it in a browser, and it *still* just reads as one plain line — nothing about it becomes a list, a heading, or anything else, until you wrap it in tags that say what it is.

contentSections.scenario:
Three attempts at marking up the word "Morning meds" as a heading: ```

Morning meds

Morning meds Morning meds ```
contentSections.question: Which of these actually makes "Morning meds" a heading, as far as the browser and a screen reader are concerned?

options.label:
Morning meds

— opening tag, content, closing tag
<h1>Morning meds — opening tag only, no closing tag
Morning meds — no tags at all

feedback.complete:
Right. An element is three parts together: the opening tag (

), the content, and the closing tag (

). All three have to be there for the browser to know where "heading" starts and stops.
feedback.unclosed: This is missing . Browsers are forgiving and will usually still render something, but the browser is left guessing where the heading actually ends — and a screen reader can announce the wrong scope entirely. It's a bug, not a style choice.
feedback.none: With no tags, this is just text sitting in the file. Nothing tells the browser it's a heading rather than a stray sentence — it'll render as an ordinary line, same size and weight as everything around it.

contentSections.concept: An HTML element is an opening tag, some content, and a matching closing tag: <tagname>content</tagname>. The tag names say what the content *is* — heading, paragraph, list — not what it looks like. That's the whole job of HTML: labeling meaning, not appearance.

contentSections.body:
Elements nest inside each other, and nesting has to close in the reverse order it opened — like parentheses. `

Take ibuprofen at 8am.

` is valid: `` opens after `

` and closes before `

` closes. `

Take ibuprofen

` is broken — `` closes *after* `

`, which is closing out of order, and browsers have to guess what you meant. Most tags come in pairs like this. A few — ``, `
`, `` — are self-closing and never wrap content, because there's nothing to put inside them.
An element is an opening tag, content, and a closing tag — all three, in the right order — and that's what tells the browser what something *is*.

contentSections.title: The skeleton every page starts with

contentSections.body:
You save a file with just `

My meds

` in it, name it page.html, and open it. It works — the heading shows up. So what are those six extra lines every real page seems to start with, and does skipping them actually break anything?

contentSections.question:
A real page starts with ``, then ``, then `...`, then `...`. If you skip all of that and just write `

My meds

` alone in the file, does the browser refuse to show it?
contentSections.hint: Browsers are built to be forgiving of missing structure — that doesn't mean the missing structure has no cost, just that the failure isn't a blank screen.
contentSections.answer: No — the browser will still render it. Browsers guess at the missing pieces and fill them in silently. But you lose real things in the process: without `<!DOCTYPE html>`, the browser can drop into an old backwards-compatibility rendering mode with different sizing rules. Without `lang="en"` on `<html>`, a screen reader doesn't know which language's pronunciation rules to use for your text. Without a real `<title>` in `<head>`, the browser tab and any bookmark just show the file name. Nothing crashes — it just quietly gets worse in ways you won't notice until something depends on them.

contentSections.body:
The standard skeleton is: ```html My medication log

My meds

``` `` tells the browser to use modern, standards-based rendering. `` names the page's language — screen readers use this to choose pronunciation, and it's one of the cheapest accessibility wins there is. `` holds metadata nobody sees directly: character encoding, the page `` (shown in the browser tab, bookmarks, and search results), and later, links to CSS. `<body>` holds everything a visitor actually sees.
The skeleton doesn't stop the page from working if you skip it — it stops the page from working *well*, for a browser, a search engine, and a screen reader.

title: Headings, paragraphs, lists and links
description: Headings form a real outline someone can navigate by, lists are for things that are actually a list, and links go somewhere real — the four elements that carry most of an ordinary page.

learningObjectives.text: Order headings h1-h6 as a hierarchy rather than picking by size
Choose <ul>/<ol>/<li> over separated paragraphs for genuinely listed content
Write a working link with a real, meaningful href

contentSections.title: Headings are an outline, not a font size

contentSections.body: A screen reader user browsing your symptom-tracking page doesn't scroll through it top to bottom — they pull up a list of every heading on the page and jump straight to the section they want, the same way you'd use a table of contents. If your headings were picked by "what size looked right" instead of what the content's rank actually is, that jump-list stops making sense.

contentSections.scenario:
A page about tracking daily symptoms has these headings, in order down the page: Option A:

Symptom Tracker

, then

Today's Entry

, then

Pain Level

, then

Sleep Quality

Option B:

Symptom Tracker

, then

Today's Entry

(because "it looked too big as h2"), then

Pain Level

(because "it needed to stand out")
contentSections.question: Which heading structure is actually correct?

options.label: Option A — nested by rank, no levels skipped
Option B — sized by how it should visually stand out
Both are fine, since headings are just for visual size

feedback.a: Right. h1 is the page's one main heading, h2s are its major sections, h3s are subsections within an h2 — a real hierarchy, with nothing skipped and nothing chosen for how big it looks.
feedback.b: This picks heading level by "how big should this look," not by what it actually is in the outline. Jumping from h1 straight to h3, then back to a second h1, produces an outline that makes no structural sense — even though every individual heading still displays fine.
feedback.both: They render differently, but only one of them describes a real, navigable outline. Size is what CSS is for — the heading level's job is rank, not appearance.

contentSections.concept: Headings (h1 through h6) describe a document's outline by rank, not by how large they should look. h1 is the page's single main heading; h2s mark its major sections; h3s mark subsections within an h2. Skipping a level (h1 straight to h3) or using two h1s to mean "important" breaks the outline a screen reader user actually navigates by — and font size, later, is CSS's job entirely.

contentSections.body: In practice: one `<h1>` per page (the page's actual subject), then `<h2>` for each major section, `<h3>` for subsections within a section, and so on down to `<h6>` if you ever need it — most pages never go past `<h3>` or `<h4>`. If a heading level *looks* wrong once you've picked it correctly, that's a CSS problem to fix with `font-size` — not a reason to reach for a different heading tag.
Pick a heading level by its rank in the outline, never by how big you want it to look.

contentSections.title: Paragraphs, lists, and links: the other 90%

contentSections.body: You're logging today's groceries: eggs, oat milk, ginger tea, paracetamol. Type it as one sentence with commas, and a screen reader announces one long run-on. Mark it up as an actual list, and it announces "list, 4 items" up front, then lets someone jump straight to item 3 if that's the one they need.

contentSections.scenario: Four ways someone might mark up that same four-item grocery list.
contentSections.question: Which of these genuinely produce a real, navigable list — not just something that visually resembles one?

items.label:
• Eggs
  • Oat milk
  • Ginger tea
  • Paracetamol

1. Eggs
  2. Oat milk
  3. Ginger tea
  4. Paracetamol

Eggs
Oat milk
Ginger tea
Paracetamol

Eggs

Oat milk

Ginger tea

Paracetamol

explanation.ul_li: Yes — <ul> (unordered list) with <li> items is a real list. A screen reader announces "list, 4 items" and lets someone navigate item by item.
explanation.ol_li: Yes — <ol> (ordered list) is the numbered version, for when the order genuinely matters (steps in a routine, ranked items). Same real list behavior, plus visible numbering.
explanation.br_sep: This only *looks* like a list, using line breaks to fake the visual layout. A screen reader has no idea it's four separate things — it just hears one paragraph with pauses in it, and there's no way to jump to item 3.
explanation.four_p: Four separate paragraphs read as four unrelated blocks of text, not one grouped list of four related items — there's no signal that they belong together at all.

contentSections.synthesis:
Visually similar isn't structurally equivalent.
and separate

tags can be made to *look* like a list with the right spacing, but only

    /
      with
    1. children actually tells the browser and a screen reader "this is one list, and here are its items."

contentSections.body: For links, `` is what makes text clickable — but the `href` has to point somewhere real. `Click here` looks like a link and behaves like one visually, but goes nowhere, which is exactly as useless to a sighted user as it is to a screen reader user who was told "link" and gets nothing. Link text should describe the destination too: "View today's symptom log" tells you something on its own; "click here" or "read more" tells you nothing if a screen reader user is scanning a page's list of links out of context, which is a common way they navigate.
A list only counts as a list if it's built from <ul>/<ol> and <li> — line breaks and separate paragraphs just fake the look of one.

title: Semantic elements, and why div isn't the answer
description: <div> renders fine and says nothing about what it contains — semantic elements like <header>, <nav>, <main> and <footer> carry real meaning a screen reader can announce, for the exact same visual result.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what a screen reader loses when a page is built entirely from <div>
Choose the correct semantic element for a page region's actual role
Judge when <div> or <span> is the genuinely correct choice, not a shortcut

contentSections.title: div says nothing; semantic tags say something

contentSections.body: You build a whole symptom-tracker page out of nested <div>s with class names like "header" and "nav" and "main-content" — it looks completely correct in the browser, matches your design exactly, and a screen reader announces every single one of them identically: "group." The class name means something to you. It means nothing to the accessibility tree.

contentSections.code:
Symptom Tracker
Today
History
Pain: 4/10
contentSections.question: This renders exactly like a real header, nav, and main content area, once styled. What's actually wrong with it?

options.label: The class names are misspelled
Every element is a generic <div> — nothing here tells a screen reader or search engine what any region actually is
Nothing is wrong — class names already communicate the meaning

feedback.spelling: The class names are spelled fine, and that's beside the point — class names exist for CSS and JavaScript to hook into, not for a screen reader to read as meaning.
feedback.no_semantics: Right. A class named "header" is just a string as far as the accessibility tree is concerned — it carries zero structural meaning. A screen reader announces every one of these as "group," indistinguishable from any other <div> on the page, no matter how descriptive the class name looks to you.
feedback.fine: It looks fine — visually, it's indistinguishable from a properly semantic version. But class names are invisible to assistive technology; they're a hook for styling and scripting, not a signal of meaning.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Nothing here is visually broken, which is exactly what makes this mistake so common — the page can look perfectly finished while still being structurally meaningless to anyone not looking at it. The fix isn't new styling, it's swapping the generic tag names for ones that actually say what each region is: <header>, <nav>, <main>.

contentSections.body:
HTML has semantic elements built for exactly these common page regions: ```html

Symptom Tracker

Today History

Pain: 4/10

© 2026

``` Same visual result once styled, but now a screen reader can announce "navigation, 2 items" and let someone jump straight to it, a search engine can tell your actual page content in `
` apart from repeated boilerplate in `
`/`
`, and a sighted developer reading the raw HTML can tell what each region is without opening a single class name.
A <div> is visually invisible and semantically invisible too — it says nothing about what it contains, no matter what you name its class.

contentSections.title: When div (or span) really is the right call

contentSections.body: None of this means <div> is a mistake to eliminate everywhere. Sometimes you genuinely just need a box to hang a background color on, with no meaning to announce at all — and reaching for a semantic tag that doesn't fit is its own kind of wrong.

contentSections.scenario: Four real situations while building a page.
contentSections.question: In which of these is a plain <div> or <span> actually the correct, honest choice — not a shortcut?

items.label: Wrapping a section purely to apply a background color with CSS, with no semantic role of its own
Wrapping one word mid-sentence to color it red, using <span>
Wrapping the site's main navigation links
Wrapping a full blog post's self-contained content

explanation.color_wrap: Correct use — if a wrapper's only job is styling, with no independent meaning to announce, <div> is exactly the right, honest tag for it. Nothing is being hidden or lost, because there was no semantic meaning to begin with.
explanation.inline_style: Also correct — <span> is <div>'s inline equivalent, for exactly this: styling a small piece of text with no meaning of its own to convey.
explanation.site_nav: This has a real semantic role — it's navigation — and <nav> exists specifically to announce that. Using <div> here is exactly the mistake from the first pod, discarding real meaning that was available for free.
explanation.article_body: A self-contained piece of content like a blog post has <article> built for precisely this case. <div> would work visually but throws away a real, easy semantic win.

contentSections.synthesis: The test isn't "does a semantic tag exist that could technically wrap this" — it's "does this region have a real, distinct role." When the honest answer is no, <div>/<span> are the correct choice, not a fallback.

contentSections.body: A rough way to decide: ask what this chunk of the page *is*, not what it looks like. Site-wide navigation is `<nav>`. The page's main content is `<main>` (only one per page). A self-contained, independently distributable piece of content — a blog post, a single symptom log entry that could stand alone — is `<article>`. A themed grouping of related content that isn't its own document is `<section>`. If none of those honestly describe it, and it's purely there for CSS or JavaScript to hook into, `<div>` (block) or `<span>` (inline) are correct — not a cop-out, just the accurate answer.
Reach for a semantic tag when the region has a real role. Reach for div/span when it genuinely doesn't — that's not laziness, that's accuracy.

title: Images, alt text and the description that carries meaning
description: An image with no alt text isn't invisible to a screen reader — it's announced as noise. Writing the description is how the meaning actually gets across.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what a screen reader announces for an image with missing versus present alt text
Write alt text that describes content or function, not "image of..."
Distinguish decorative images (alt="") from informative ones

contentSections.title: Alt text is not optional decoration

contentSections.body: You post a photo of a rash to a symptom-tracking page, no alt attribute. A sighted visitor sees the photo instantly. A screen reader user hears the file name — "IMG dash 4821 dot j p g" — read out loud, letter by letter, which tells them precisely nothing about what's actually in the image.

contentSections.scenario: Four ways the same photo of a swollen ankle might be marked up: 1. `` 2. `` 3. `` 4. ``
contentSections.question: Which version actually gives a screen reader user something useful?

options.label: Version 4 — a specific, concrete description
Version 1 — no alt attribute at all
Version 2 — alt="image"

feedback.v4: Right. Version 4 tells you what's actually in the photo — specific enough to be useful for someone tracking symptoms over time, without needing to see the image at all.
feedback.v1: With no alt attribute, most screen readers fall back to reading the file name — "IMG underscore 4821 dot j p g" — which conveys zero medical information.
feedback.v2: alt="image" is technically present but says nothing beyond confirming there is, in fact, an image there. It's barely better than no alt text at all — it fills the requirement without doing the job.

contentSections.mechanism: A screen reader announces whatever string is in the `alt` attribute, verbatim, in place of the image. Missing alt falls back to the file name. A present-but-vague alt ("image") technically satisfies "has an alt attribute" without actually conveying anything. Only a specific, content-describing alt text does the job the attribute exists for.

contentSections.body: `alt` text should describe what the image actually shows or does, as if you were briefly describing it to someone on the phone: "Left ankle, visibly swollen and bruised along the outer side" — not "image of ankle" (the word "image" is redundant; screen readers already announce that it's an image before reading the alt text) and not "IMG_4821" (meaningless to anyone). If the image is functional — a magnifying glass icon that's actually a search button — describe the *function*, not the picture: `alt="Search"`, not `alt="magnifying glass icon"`.
Write alt text like you're describing the image over the phone — specific and useful, never "image of..." and never the file name.

contentSections.title: Decorative vs informative, and the empty alt trick

contentSections.body: A thin decorative line-drawing divider sits between two sections of your page, purely for visual spacing — no information in it at all. Giving it a real description ("squiggly decorative line") doesn't help anyone; it's just noise a screen reader user now has to sit through before reaching the actual content.

contentSections.intro: You're marking up three images on a medication page: a photo of the actual pill (informative), a decorative divider graphic (purely visual, no content), and a printer icon that's really a "print this page" button (functional).

fields.prompt: Photo of the actual pill, used so the patient can visually confirm they have the right medication
options: alt="White oval tablet, imprinted 'M400' on one side"
fields.correctValue: alt="White oval tablet, imprinted 'M400' on one side"
fields.feedback: This image carries real information someone needs (to visually confirm the right pill) — it needs a genuine, specific description, not an empty or file-name alt.

fields.prompt: A purely decorative line-drawing graphic between two sections, no content of its own
fields.feedback: An empty alt="" tells screen readers to skip the image entirely — exactly right for pure decoration with nothing to announce. Leaving the attribute off entirely instead risks the file-name fallback, which is worse, not neutral.

fields.prompt: A printer icon that's actually a clickable "print this page" button
fields.feedback: For a functional image (one that's really a button or link), describe what it *does*, not what it looks like — "printer icon" tells a screen reader user nothing about what clicking it will do.

contentSections.synthesis: Three different rules for three different roles: informative images get a real, specific description; purely decorative ones get alt="" (never no attribute at all — that risks the meaningless file-name fallback); functional images describe the action, not the icon.

contentSections.body: One easy test for whether an image is decorative: if you deleted it, would the page lose any actual information? A stock background pattern — no. A photo you're using to document a symptom, or an icon that's the only visual cue for a button's function — yes. `alt=""` (present but empty) is the correct, deliberate way to mark something decorative; it tells screen readers to skip past it silently, which is different from — and better than — leaving the attribute off and letting the file name leak through instead.
alt="" on purpose means "skip this, it's decoration." No alt attribute at all means "guess from the file name" — and that guess is always worse.

title: Forms: asking the user for something
description: A form field without a real <label> can look perfectly fine and still be nearly unusable — for a screen reader user, for someone whose hands shake, and for anyone who tabs through fields by keyboard.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why placeholder text is not a substitute for a <label>
Link a <label> to its <input> correctly using for/id
Choose an input type and button wording appropriate to what's being asked

contentSections.title: A field with no question attached

contentSections.body: You build a symptom-log form: a text box with faint gray placeholder text reading "Pain level, 0-10" inside it. The moment someone clicks in and starts typing, that placeholder vanishes — and if their hand shakes and the page scrolls, or they tab away and come back, there's no longer anything on screen telling them what this field was even asking.

contentSections.question: This looks like a perfectly normal form field. What's actually missing, and why does it matter beyond looks?

options.label: Nothing — placeholder text is a valid way to label a field
A <label> element — placeholder text disappears on focus and isn't reliably announced by screen readers
The input needs a border to look more like a text box

feedback.fine: It looks fine and is a genuinely common mistake, which is exactly the problem — it works well enough that it's easy to never notice what's missing until someone who relies on it tells you.
feedback.no_label: Right. There's no <label> here at all — placeholder text is a hint shown inside an empty field, not a persistent, reliably-announced label. It vanishes the moment someone starts typing, and some screen readers don't announce it consistently in the first place.
feedback.border: Visual styling isn't the issue here at all — this is about whether the field's *purpose* is ever communicated in a durable way, not how it looks.

contentSections.flawExplanation:
The fix is a real <label>, connected to the input, that stays on screen the whole time regardless of what's typed:

```html
<label for="painLevel">Pain level, 0-10</label>
<input type="text" id="painLevel">
```

The `for` attribute on the label and the `id` on the input have to match exactly — that's what links them, and it's what lets a screen reader announce the label the moment the field receives focus, not just while it happens to be empty.

contentSections.body: A `<label>` connected via matching `for`/`id` does more than announce the field's purpose to a screen reader — clicking the label text itself moves focus into (or toggles) the input, which is a real, tangible benefit for anyone with limited fine motor control aiming for a small checkbox. Placeholder text can still be useful *in addition to* a label — as a hint about format, like "e.g. 400mg" — but it should never be the only thing standing in for a label.
Placeholder text disappears the moment someone types. A <label> stays — connect it with a matching for/id, always.

contentSections.title: Submitting a form and what the button says

contentSections.body: A screen reader user often pulls up a list of every button on a page to decide what to do next, completely out of context from the surrounding text. A button labeled "Submit" tells them nothing at that point. A button labeled "Save medication log" tells them exactly what pressing it will do.

contentSections.scenario: A medication-log form has a phone number field, a dose-in-mg number field, and a submit button.
contentSections.question: Which of these choices genuinely help the person filling out the form, beyond just working?

items.label: <input type="tel"> for the phone number, instead of type="text"
<input type="number"> for the dose in mg, instead of type="text"
A button reading "Save medication log" instead of "Submit"
Using type="text" for every field, including the phone number and dose

explanation.tel_input: Real benefit — on a phone, type="tel" brings up the numeric phone keypad instead of the full alphabet keyboard, which is faster and less error-prone one-handed or with limited dexterity.
explanation.number_input: Also a real benefit — type="number" brings up a numeric keypad on mobile and lets the browser reject non-numeric input before it's even submitted, catching a typo earlier than a server-side check would.
explanation.specific_button: A specific label describes the actual action, useful to everyone but especially to someone navigating by a list of buttons out of context — "Submit" describes nothing about what will happen.
explanation.text_everything: type="text" technically accepts anything typed, including a phone number or a dose — but it throws away the better keyboard and built-in validation the more specific types offer for free.

contentSections.synthesis: None of these choices change whether the form *works* — a plain type="text" field would still accept a phone number. They change how much friction the form has for whoever's actually filling it in, particularly one-handed, on a phone, or by screen reader.

contentSections.body: Beyond `tel` and `number`, common input types include `email` (email keyboard on mobile, basic format checking), `checkbox` (yes/no, like "took medication today"), and `date`. Marking a field `required` tells the browser to block submission until it's filled in, giving immediate feedback before a round trip to a server. And `<button type="submit">Save medication log</button>` — specific wording, not a generic "Submit" — closes the loop on a form that's not just functional but actually easy to use under real conditions: one hand, low light, a bad day.
The right input type and a specific button label cost nothing extra to write and remove real friction for whoever's actually filling the form out.

title: Practice — Fix the Semantics of Eight Markup Snippets
description: Eight drills, no new concepts: given a snippet that renders correctly but says the wrong thing (or nothing) structurally, find and fix the semantic problem.

learningObjectives.text: Identify missing or incorrect semantic structure in real markup snippets

contentSections.title: Eight snippets, the same handful of rules

contentSections.body: Every one of these traces back to something from this module: an unclosed or misordered tag, a heading picked for size instead of rank, a div standing in for a role that had a real semantic tag available, missing or meaningless alt text, or a form field with no connected label.
Almost every semantic bug in this module comes down to one question: is there a tag here that already exists to say this, that I replaced with something generic?

title: Lab — Build a Semantic Page About Something You Care About
description: A real page, about something genuinely yours — built with correct structure from the ground up, then checked the way this module has been teaching you to check it: an outline built from your headings, and a screen reader (or its text-only equivalent) reading it back to you.

learningObjectives.text: Structure a real page with the correct html/head/body skeleton and semantic regions
Use headings, lists, links, images and a form correctly and semantically together
Verify a page's structure by reconstructing its outline from headings alone

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Everything in this module has been building toward one page you build for real: not a snippet to fix, but a whole document — structured correctly from the skeleton up, using headings that form a real outline, at least one real list, at least one image with real alt text, and a small form, all wrapped in semantic regions instead of generic divs.

contentSections.title: Build a semantic page about something you care about
contentSections.brief: Pick a real subject: a hobby, a condition you track, a project, a book you're re-reading, anything genuinely yours. Build a single HTML page about it — not a mockup, a real .html file you can open in a browser — using every element this module covered, structured so the page's meaning is clear even with all styling stripped away.
contentSections.deliverable: A page that reads correctly with a screen reader and headings turned into an outline.

stages.title: Skeleton and outline
stages.instructions: Start from the standard <!DOCTYPE html>/<html lang="en">/<head>/<body> skeleton, with a real <title>. Before writing any content, write out your planned heading structure as a simple outline in plain English (one <h1>, then h2s for major sections, h3s for subsections) — get the ranks right before you touch a single sentence of real content.
stages.checkpoint: You have a complete skeleton and a written heading outline with no skipped levels and exactly one h1.

stages.title: Content: headings, paragraphs, a list, a link
stages.instructions: Fill in real content following your outline: headings from stage 1, paragraphs of real text, at least one genuine <ul> or <ol> list (not a paragraph with line breaks), and at least one link with a real href and descriptive link text (not "click here").
stages.checkpoint: Every heading matches your planned outline, the list is built from <ul>/<ol> and <li>, and the link's text describes its destination.

stages.title: An image and a small form, wrapped semantically
stages.instructions: Add one image with alt text following lesson 4's rules (a real description if it's informative, alt="" if it's purely decorative) and a small form with at least one field, using a real <label> connected via matching for/id (not a placeholder standing in alone). Then wrap the whole page in semantic regions — <header>, <nav> if relevant, <main>, <footer> — instead of leaving it as bare divs or ungrouped content.
stages.checkpoint: The image has correct alt text for its role, the form field has a connected label, and the page uses semantic region elements instead of generic divs.

stages.title: Check it the way a screen reader user would
stages.instructions: Reconstruct your page's outline from its headings alone (list every heading in order, with its level) and confirm it matches what you planned in stage 1. Then read through the page top to bottom imagining you can't see it — for each image, is the alt text alone enough to know what it shows or does? For the form field, is the label enough to know what's being asked, with no placeholder as backup? Fix anything that fails either check before calling it done.
stages.checkpoint: Your reconstructed heading outline matches stage 1's plan, and every image and form field passes the no-visual-context check.

rubric.criterion: The skeleton and metadata are complete
rubric.meets: DOCTYPE, lang attribute, and a real, specific <title> are all present.

rubric.criterion: Headings form a real, navigable outline
rubric.meets: Exactly one h1, no skipped levels, ranks reflect actual structure rather than desired size.

rubric.criterion: Lists and links are used correctly
rubric.meets: At least one real <ul>/<ol> list, and link text that describes its destination rather than "click here."

rubric.criterion: The image's alt text matches its actual role
rubric.meets: A real, specific description for informative content, or alt="" for purely decorative images.

rubric.criterion: The form field has a connected label
rubric.meets: A <label> linked via matching for/id, not a placeholder used alone as the only label.

rubric.criterion: Semantic regions replace generic divs where a real role exists
rubric.meets: header/nav/main/footer used for regions that actually have that role, not left as unlabeled divs.

contentSections.body: A page that passes the "read it with the styling stripped away" test is a page that was actually built with structure, not just decorated to look like it.

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — HTML: Structure and Meaning

questions.from: This module — HTML: Structure and Meaning
questions.prompt: What three parts make up a complete HTML element?

options.label: A tag name, a class, and an id
An opening tag, content, and a matching closing tag
A DOCTYPE, an html tag, and a body tag

questions.explanation: <tagname>content</tagname> — opening tag, content, closing tag, all three present and in order. That's what tells the browser where the element starts and stops.

questions.from: This module — HTML: Structure and Meaning
questions.prompt:
A page has

Tracker

followed directly by

Today

, with no

in between. What's wrong with this?

options.label: Nothing — h3 just makes it a smaller heading
It skips a heading level, breaking the outline a screen reader user navigates by
You can't use h3 without also using h2 and h1 in the same element

questions.explanation: Heading levels are a rank in the document's outline, not a font-size picker. Skipping from h1 to h3 leaves a gap in that outline, even though both headings render fine on their own.

questions.from: This module — HTML: Structure and Meaning
questions.prompt: Why does a page built entirely from <div class="nav"> instead of <nav> lose something, even if it looks identical once styled?

options.label: Class names are invisible to screen readers — <div> announces as generic "group" regardless of its class
<div> renders slower than <nav>
Nothing is actually lost — class names carry the same meaning as a semantic tag

questions.explanation: Class names exist for CSS and JavaScript to hook into — they carry zero meaning to a screen reader. Only the tag name itself (<nav> vs <div>) is announced as structural information.

questions.from: This module — HTML: Structure and Meaning
questions.prompt: What does alt="" (present but empty) tell a screen reader, and how is that different from leaving the alt attribute off entirely?

options.label: They're identical — both cause the image to be skipped
alt="" means "skip this on purpose, it's decorative"; a missing attribute risks the image's file name being read aloud instead
alt="" is invalid HTML and will cause an error

questions.explanation: An empty alt is a deliberate signal to skip a purely decorative image. Omitting the attribute entirely is not the same — many screen readers fall back to announcing the file name instead, which is worse, not neutral.

questions.from: Previous module — Lists and Records
questions.prompt: From Lists and Records: what does a list (array) let you do that a set of separate individually-named variables doesn't?

options.label: Hold many values under one name, so you can loop through them or work with the whole group at once
Store a value with no type at all
Skip needing a variable name entirely

questions.explanation: A list groups many related values under one name, which is what makes looping over them — or passing the whole collection around at once — possible in the first place.

questions.from: Previous module — Lists and Records
questions.prompt: From Lists and Records: a list has 5 items. What index gets you the first one, and what happens if you ask for index 5?

options.label: Index 1 gets the first item; index 5 gets the last one
Index 0 gets the first item; index 5 is past the end (a 5-item list runs 0 through 4)
Index 0 gets the first item; index 5 also works and just wraps back to the start

questions.explanation: Lists are zero-indexed — the first item is index 0, and a 5-item list's valid indexes run 0 through 4. Index 5 is one past the end, the classic off-by-one mistake.

questions.from: Previous module — Lists and Records
questions.prompt: From Lists and Records: what's a record (object) for, that a plain list of values isn't?

options.label: Describing one thing with several named fields, instead of positions you'd have to remember the order of
Storing values faster than a list can
Holding only numbers, never text

questions.explanation: A record holds named fields (name, dose, time) so you look values up by name rather than remembering that position 2 in a list always means "dose." That naming is the entire point.

questions.from: Previous module — Lists and Records
questions.prompt: From Lists and Records: what shape is most real-world structured data — a symptom log with many entries, each with several fields?

options.label: One long list of plain numbers
A list of records — each item in the list is itself a record with named fields
A single record with one field per day

questions.explanation: A list of records — each entry is its own record (date, pain level, notes), and the list holds many of them. This shape is what almost all real tracked data actually looks like.

options.label: Nothing — the loop just runs once and stops
It runs forever, freezing the program (an infinite loop)
JavaScript automatically stops it after a few seconds

questions.explanation: A loop that checks a condition which never flips keeps running indefinitely — an infinite loop — with nothing built into the language to rescue you from it automatically.

options.label: + always converts numbers into text
With a string on either side, + joins as text instead of adding
This is a bug in JavaScript with no real explanation

questions.explanation: + is uniquely overloaded between addition and text-joining. A string on either side tips it toward joining as text — the same quiet type-coercion behavior that makes mixed-type arithmetic worth double-checking.
