title: Selectors: choosing what to style
description: A CSS rule only ever does one thing: match some elements, apply some styles. Picking a selector that's too broad is the single most common way a beginner's one small change breaks something else on the page.

learningObjectives.text: Choose an element, class, or id selector appropriate to how broadly a style should apply
Explain why an overly broad selector affects elements you didn't intend to change
Predict which of two conflicting rules wins, based on specificity

contentSections.title: Picking one thing without picking everything

contentSections.body: You want just the low-battery warning text on your spoon-tracker page to turn red. You write `p { color: red; }` to do it — and every single paragraph on the page turns red with it, because that selector never said "just this one," it said "every paragraph, everywhere."

contentSections.scenario:
The page has one warning paragraph: `

Low spoons — consider resting.

`, among several other ordinary paragraphs.
contentSections.question: Which selector turns only the warning paragraph red, leaving the others untouched?

options.label: p { color: red; }
.warning { color: red; }
* { color: red; }

feedback.element:
This matches every

on the page, regardless of class — it turns all paragraphs red, not just the warning.
feedback.class: Right. A class selector (the dot, `.warning`) matches only elements carrying that exact class attribute — everything else on the page is untouched.
feedback.universal: The universal selector (*) matches literally everything on the page — every element, of every kind. It's the broadest possible selector, not a narrow one.

contentSections.concept: A selector's job is to say exactly what a rule applies to. An element selector (`p`) matches every element of that tag, everywhere. A class selector (`.warning`) matches only elements carrying that class, however many or few there are. Picking a selector broader than what you actually mean to style is the single most common cause of "I changed one thing and three other things also changed."

contentSections.body: The three you'll use constantly: an **element selector** (`p`, `h1`, `button`) matches every element of that tag. A **class selector** (`.warning`, written with a dot) matches every element carrying `class="warning"`, and the same class can be reused on as many elements as you want. An **id selector** (`#pageHeader`, written with a hash) matches the one element carrying `id="pageHeader"` — ids are meant to be unique per page, used for one specific element, not a repeatable group. When in doubt: reach for a class, since you'll almost always want to reuse a style on more than one thing eventually.
A selector is a promise about scope. Pick the narrowest one that actually matches what you mean to style.

contentSections.title: Specificity: when two rules disagree

contentSections.body: You write `p { color: black; }` at the top of your stylesheet, then `.warning { color: red; }` further down, targeting the exact same paragraph. Which wins isn't about which one you wrote more recently, and it isn't a coin flip — CSS has an actual rule for this.

contentSections.question: The text renders red, not black. Why does .warning win here?

options.label: Class selectors always beat element selectors, regardless of order
Whichever rule is written second always wins, no matter what kind of selector it is
It's random — CSS doesn't have a defined rule for this

feedback.specificity: Right. A class selector is more specific than a plain element selector, and higher specificity wins regardless of which rule was written first or last.
feedback.order_only: Order only decides the winner when two rules have equal specificity — it's the tiebreaker, not the main rule. Here, .warning wins because it's more specific, not because it comes later.
feedback.random: CSS has a fully defined, deterministic system for this called specificity — nothing about which style wins is left to chance.

contentSections.mechanism: Every selector has a specificity score: id selectors score highest, class selectors next, element selectors lowest. When two rules target the same element, the higher-specificity rule wins, no matter which was written first. Only when specificity is exactly tied does write-order become the tiebreaker — the later rule wins.

contentSections.body: Rough order, low to high: element selectors (`p`) < class selectors (`.warning`) < id selectors (`#header`). A rule using `#header` will beat a conflicting rule using `.warning` or `p`, even if the id rule is written first in the file. This is exactly why a lot of real CSS avoids id selectors for styling — they're so specific that they're hard to override later, which becomes its own kind of maintenance headache.
When two rules conflict, the more specific selector wins — not the one written later, unless specificity is tied.

title: The box model, which explains most confusion
description: Every element on a page is a rectangular box made of four stacked layers — and most "why is this bigger/smaller/further away than I typed" confusion traces back to one of them.

learningObjectives.text: Name the four layers of the box model, from innermost to outermost
Predict a box's rendered width given its content width, padding and border
Explain what box-sizing: border-box changes and why it's commonly set

contentSections.title: Every element is a box, whether you wanted it to be or not

contentSections.body: You set a background color on a div holding a short sentence, expecting a tight box hugging the text. Instead there's a big empty-looking colored rectangle around it — nothing is broken, that's genuinely how much space the box is taking up, once you count everything that isn't the text itself.

contentSections.scenario: A box has: text content, 20px of padding around that content, a 2px border around the padding, and 10px of margin outside the border.
contentSections.question: Which layer is the space between the box's border and whatever's next to it — invisible, and never gets a background color?

options.label: Padding
Margin
Border

feedback.padding: Padding is inside the border, between the content and the border — it does get the element's background color, which is exactly why a padded box looks bigger than its text.
feedback.margin: Right. Margin is the outermost layer, pushing other elements away — it's always transparent, never picks up a background color, and exists purely to create space between this box and its neighbors.
feedback.border: The border is a visible line between padding and margin — it's not invisible, and it's not what creates spacing to neighboring elements (margin does that).

contentSections.concept: Every element is four nested layers, innermost to outermost: content (the text or child elements), padding (space inside the border, same background as the box), border (a visible line), and margin (invisible space outside the border, pushing neighbors away). A background color fills content and padding, stops at the border, and never touches margin — which is exactly why a box with lots of padding looks much bigger than its actual text.

contentSections.body: This is the **box model**, and it explains most "why does this look bigger/smaller than I expected" confusion once you know to check it: is the extra space padding (colored, inside the border) or margin (transparent, outside it)? `padding: 20px;` and `margin: 20px;` look identical in a screenshot description but do completely different things — one grows the visible colored box, the other just pushes it away from its neighbors.
Content, padding, border, margin — inside to outside. Padding is colored and inside the border; margin is invisible space outside it.

contentSections.title: Width you set isn't the width you get (unless you fix that)

contentSections.body: You set `width: 200px` on three cards meant to sit in a neat row. Add `padding: 20px` and a `border: 2px solid` to make them look nicer, and suddenly they don't fit in the row anymore — each one is actually 244px wide now, not 200px, and nothing you typed said 244.

contentSections.question: This card renders wider than 200px. What's actually going on?

options.label: By default, width sets only the content's width — padding and border are added on top of it
There's a typo somewhere in the padding or border value
Browsers round width up unpredictably

feedback.content_box: Right. By default (content-box sizing), `width` only sets the content layer's width. Padding and border get added on top: 200 (content) + 20+20 (padding both sides) + 2+2 (border both sides) = 244px total rendered width.
feedback.typo: The numbers are all valid, correctly-formatted CSS — this isn't a syntax mistake, it's the default sizing behavior working exactly as designed, just not as most beginners expect.
feedback.rounding: This has nothing to do with rounding — the extra 44px is fully accounted for by padding and border being added on top of the content width, not an unpredictable browser quirk.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix, and something most real projects set globally on every element: `box-sizing: border-box;`. With border-box, `width: 200px` means the *total* rendered width, including padding and border — the content area shrinks to make room for them instead of the box growing past what you typed. It's one line, usually set once at the top of a stylesheet (`* { box-sizing: border-box; }`), and it removes an entire category of "why is this the wrong size" confusion.

contentSections.body: `box-sizing: content-box` (the default) means `width` sets only the content. `box-sizing: border-box` means `width` sets the whole box — content shrinks to fit padding and border inside that total. Almost every real project sets `box-sizing: border-box` globally near the top of its CSS, because "the number I typed is the number I get" is simply less confusing to build with than the default.
By default, width is content-only — padding and border are added on top. box-sizing: border-box makes width mean the whole box instead.

title: Layout with flexbox, without memorising everything
description: Flexbox turns a handful of child elements into a row (or column) you can space, align and wrap with a small number of properties on the parent — no floats, no manual positioning math.

learningObjectives.text: Apply display: flex and predict its default row layout
Use justify-content and align-items to control spacing and alignment
Use flex-wrap and gap to keep a row from overflowing on a narrow screen

contentSections.title: display: flex turns children into a row, by default

contentSections.body: Your navigation links — Home, Today, History — are stacked one on top of the other, because that's just how block-level elements sit by default, one below the next. You want them in a horizontal row instead, and there's one property on the parent that does it.

contentSections.scenario:
```html
Home Today History
```
contentSections.question: Which CSS rule, applied to <nav>, arranges the three links in a horizontal row?

options.label: nav { display: flex; }
a { display: flex; }
nav { direction: horizontal; }

feedback.flex: Right. display: flex on the parent (<nav>) turns its direct children into a flex row by default — no direction needs to be specified for the default behavior.
feedback.flex_children: display: flex has to go on the parent whose children you want arranged, not on the children themselves — setting it on <a> arranges each link's own (nonexistent) children, doing nothing visible here.
feedback.direction: There's no CSS property called direction for this — the property that exists is flex-direction, and it only has an effect on an element that's already display: flex.

contentSections.concept: display: flex goes on the parent element, and it changes how that parent arranges its direct children: by default, into a horizontal row, each one only as wide as its content needs. This is the single most useful layout tool for exactly the case that trips up beginners constantly — getting a handful of things to sit next to each other instead of stacking.

contentSections.body: Once a parent is `display: flex`, its children are called **flex items**, and a small set of properties on the parent controls how they're arranged: `justify-content` controls spacing along the row (`flex-start`, `center`, `space-between`, `space-around`), and `align-items` controls alignment across the row's height (`flex-start`, `center`, `stretch`). `justify-content: space-between` — links pushed to the far edges with even space between them — is one of the most common real layouts you'll reach for.
display: flex on the parent turns its children into a row by default — justify-content and align-items control the spacing and alignment inside it.

contentSections.title: Wrapping, growing, and the two properties that cover most cases

contentSections.body: Your three nav links fit fine in a row on your laptop. Open the same page on a phone, in bed, one-handed, and the row is too narrow — the links either get crushed together or spill off the edge of the screen, because a flex row doesn't wrap onto a second line unless you tell it to.

contentSections.scenario: A flex row of three buttons needs to still look reasonable on a narrow phone screen, without the developer writing separate layout code for mobile.
contentSections.question: Which of these genuinely help a flex row behave reasonably when the screen gets narrow?

items.label: flex-wrap: wrap; — lets items drop to a second line instead of overflowing or crushing
gap: 12px; — consistent spacing between items, without margin hacks on each child
Leaving flex-wrap at its default (nowrap) and hoping the buttons shrink to fit
Giving each button a large fixed pixel width regardless of screen size

explanation.flex_wrap: Real fix — by default, flex items are squeezed to fit on one line (which can crush their content) or overflow the container. flex-wrap: wrap lets extra items flow onto additional lines instead.
explanation.gap: Real, useful improvement — gap adds consistent space between flex items without the classic margin-collapsing headaches of margin on individual children, and it works the same whether the row wraps or not.
explanation.no_wrap_default: The default (nowrap) doesn't shrink items to fit gracefully — depending on their content, they can get squeezed unreadably thin or simply overflow the container's edge.
explanation.fixed_px_children: A large fixed pixel width per button is the opposite of adaptable — on a genuinely narrow screen, fixed-width children are exactly what forces overflow or crushing in the first place.

contentSections.synthesis: flex-wrap: wrap and gap are two of the highest-value, lowest-effort properties in flexbox — they cost one line each and directly fix the "looked fine on my laptop, breaks on a phone" problem that's extremely common with a row of flex items.

contentSections.body: flex-wrap: wrap and gap are the two properties that turn a flex row from "works on my screen" into "works on most screens."

title: Colour, contrast and text that people can actually read
description: Contrast isn't a design preference — it's a measurable ratio with a real minimum, and color alone is never a safe way to communicate something important.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what a contrast ratio measures and the WCAG AA minimum for normal text
Judge whether a color pairing likely passes or fails contrast requirements
Identify when color alone is being used as the only signal, and what to pair it with

contentSections.title: Contrast isn't a preference, it's a ratio

contentSections.body: Light gray text on a white background reads as clean and modern on your monitor, in good light, with rested eyes. On a phone screen in bed with the brightness turned down, or for someone with light sensitivity or low vision, that same gray-on-white can be nearly unreadable — and this isn't a matter of taste, it's a measurable number called contrast ratio.

contentSections.scenario: WCAG (the standard accessibility guideline) sets a minimum contrast ratio for normal-sized body text to count as accessible — measured as a ratio like 4.5:1, where higher means more contrast between text and background.
contentSections.question: What's the WCAG AA minimum contrast ratio for normal-sized text?
contentSections.explanation: 4.5:1 for normal text (3:1 is allowed for large or bold text, which is naturally easier to read at lower contrast). Pure black on pure white is about 21:1 — the maximum possible — so 4.5:1 is a real minimum, not the ceiling. A lot of "clean, minimal" light-gray-on-white designs land well under 3:1, which fails outright, not just looks slightly less crisp.

contentSections.body: Contrast ratio compares the luminance (brightness) of text against its background — free tools (search "contrast checker") let you paste in two hex colors and get the exact ratio, no manual calculation required. The rule of thumb worth internalizing: if you're picking a lighter gray for text because pure black "feels too harsh," check the ratio before shipping it — "feels softer to me, on my screen, right now" and "passes 4.5:1 for everyone" are two different, sometimes conflicting things.
4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text — contrast has an actual number attached to it, not just a look.

contentSections.title: Color alone can't be the only signal

contentSections.body: A medication form turns a field's border red when something's invalid — no icon, no text, just the color change. For a colorblind user, or someone glancing at a low-brightness phone screen, that red border can look identical to the ordinary gray one, and the only signal that something needs fixing disappears entirely.

contentSections.scenario: A form needs to show that the "dose" field has an invalid value.
contentSections.question: Which of these approaches actually communicate the error to someone who can't reliably distinguish the color difference?

items.label: Turning the field's border red, with nothing else changed
Red border plus a warning icon next to the field
Red border plus the text "Enter a dose between 1 and 999" below the field
A dashed border pattern plus an icon, with no color change at all

explanation.red_only: Color is the only signal here — remove the ability to distinguish red from gray (colorblindness, a dim screen, grayscale mode) and the field looks completely unremarkable, with no indication anything's wrong.
explanation.red_plus_icon: The icon is a second, non-color signal that survives even if the color difference doesn't register — someone still sees *something* marking the field.
explanation.red_plus_text: Actual text describing the problem is the strongest signal of all — it doesn't rely on color, shape, or icon recognition, just reading, and it also says what's wrong, not just that something is.
explanation.shape_change: A shape or pattern change works as a non-color signal too — the point isn't that color is forbidden, it's that at least one non-color signal has to be present alongside it.

contentSections.synthesis: The rule isn't "never use color" — color is a genuinely useful, fast signal for people who can see it clearly. The rule is that color can never be the *only* signal, because for a real share of users, it won't register at all.

contentSections.body: This shows up constantly beyond error states: a chart distinguishing categories by color alone (add patterns or labels), a status dot with no accompanying text ("online"/"offline"), a "required field" marked only by a colored asterisk with no other cue. The fix is almost always cheap — one icon, one label, one pattern — and it's the difference between information that reaches everyone and information that reaches only people who can currently, reliably tell two colors apart.
Color can support a signal, but it can never be the only one — pair it with text, an icon, or a shape.

title: Responsive: the same page on a phone in bed
description: A page built with fixed pixel widths looks fine on the screen you built it on and breaks the moment the screen is a different size — which, for this audience, is most of the time.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a fixed pixel width causes horizontal overflow on a narrower screen
Use relative units and max-width instead of fixed pixel widths for flexible layout
Write a media query that changes layout below a given screen width

contentSections.title: Fixed pixel widths break the moment the screen doesn't match

contentSections.body: You build your page on a laptop with a 1440px-wide screen, set the main content area to `width: 1000px`, and it looks great. Someone opens the same page on their phone, propped up in bed, with a 375px-wide screen — and now there's a page nearly three times wider than the screen, forcing horizontal scrolling just to read a sentence.

contentSections.question: On a 375px-wide phone screen, what actually happens?

options.label: The browser automatically shrinks it to fit the screen
The box stays 1000px wide regardless of screen size, causing horizontal overflow and scrolling
The page fails to load at all

feedback.auto_shrink: Browsers don't shrink a fixed pixel value to fit — width: 1000px means exactly 1000px, on any screen, unless something else (like a media query) explicitly overrides it at that size.
feedback.overflow: Right. A fixed width is fixed — it doesn't know or care how wide the screen actually is. On a screen narrower than the box, the result is horizontal overflow: the user has to scroll sideways to see content that should have just fit.
feedback.fail: Nothing about a too-wide box causes the page to fail to load — it renders exactly as instructed, just wider than the visible screen, which is a layout problem, not a loading one.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix usually isn't a fixed width at all, but a maximum width that yields to a narrower screen: `max-width: 1000px; width: 100%;` — the box grows up to 1000px on a wide screen, but shrinks to fit 100% of whatever screen it's actually on when that's narrower. This one change is most of what "responsive" means for a simple page.

contentSections.body: `width: 100%` (relative to the parent) combined with `max-width: 1000px` (a ceiling) is the pattern that replaces most fixed-pixel-width mistakes: the box is never wider than 1000px on a big screen, and never wider than its available space on a small one. A `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` tag in `<head>` is also required — without it, mobile browsers assume a desktop-width page and shrink the whole thing to fit, making text microscopic rather than actually reflowing it.
A fixed pixel width doesn't shrink to fit a narrower screen — it just overflows. max-width plus a relative width fixes it.

contentSections.title: Media queries: different rules at different sizes

contentSections.body: A horizontal row of nav links works well on a laptop screen but is genuinely cramped on a phone — not broken exactly, just worse. You want the exact same nav to become a stacked vertical list once the screen drops below a certain width, without maintaining two separate pages.

contentSections.intro: You want <nav> to be a horizontal flex row normally, but switch to a stacked column once the screen is 480px wide or narrower.

fields.prompt: What goes inside the parentheses to target screens 480px wide or narrower?
fields.feedback: max-width: 480px means "apply this when the screen is 480px or narrower" — it's a ceiling on the width the rule targets, matching everything at or below it.

fields.prompt: Inside that media query, which property switches the nav from a row to a stacked column?
fields.feedback: flex-direction: column re-stacks the same flex children vertically instead of horizontally — the nav is still a real flex container, just laid out along the other axis.

fields.prompt: How is a media query written, wrapping a normal CSS rule inside it?
fields.feedback: @media (condition) { ...normal rules... } — the media query wraps ordinary CSS rules, which only apply when the condition inside the parentheses is true.

contentSections.body: You can add as many `@media` blocks as you need, each with its own breakpoint, and they layer on top of your base styles rather than replacing the whole stylesheet. A common, low-effort starting point is a single breakpoint around 600px ("phone-sized") — you don't need to handle every possible screen width precisely, just make sure the layout doesn't break at the sizes people actually use.
@media (max-width: ...) { } lets one page adapt its layout below a given width — no second version of the page required.

title: Practice — Achieve Eight Stated Layouts

learningObjectives.text: Choose the correct CSS property or selector to achieve a specific, stated visual result

contentSections.title: Eight layouts, the same handful of rules

contentSections.body: Every one of these traces back to something from this module: selector scope and specificity, the box model and box-sizing, flexbox's row-by-default plus wrap and gap, contrast as a real number, and relative sizing that survives a narrower screen.
Almost every layout surprise in this module comes down to one question: did I check the box model, the specificity, or the screen width I'm assuming?

title: Lab — Style Your Page to a Stated Design
description: Take the semantic page from last module's lab and style it to a small, concrete design brief — then check it the way this module has been teaching you to check it: measured contrast, and the page zoomed to 400%.

learningObjectives.text: Apply selectors, the box model and box-sizing correctly to a real page
Lay out a page region with flexbox, including wrapping behavior
Verify a real page against a stated contrast requirement and at 400% zoom

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This is the same page you built last module — the one with real headings, a list, an image, a form — now getting an actual design pass: colors, a flex-based layout for at least one region, spacing that makes sense, and a check against two hard requirements instead of just "does it look nice to me right now."

contentSections.title: Style your page to a stated design
contentSections.brief: Using the semantic page you built in the last module's lab (or a similar page if you're starting fresh), apply a real design: a small, deliberate color palette, box-model-aware spacing, at least one flexbox-laid-out region, and layout that survives both a narrow screen and heavy zoom, not just your current window size.

stages.title: Selectors and a deliberate color palette
stages.instructions: Pick 2-3 colors total (a background, a text color, one accent) and write CSS rules using classes for anything you'll want to reuse, ids only for genuinely unique elements. Before finalizing your text/background pairing, check its contrast ratio with a contrast checker tool and confirm it meets 4.5:1 for normal text.
stages.checkpoint: Your main text/background pairing measurably passes 4.5:1 contrast, checked with a real tool, not eyeballed.

stages.title: Box model spacing, on purpose
stages.instructions: Set box-sizing: border-box globally. Add padding and margin deliberately to at least two elements — padding for space inside a box's background, margin for space between boxes — and be able to say, for each one, which layer you used and why.
stages.checkpoint: box-sizing: border-box is set globally, and padding vs margin were each chosen deliberately, not interchangeably.

stages.title: Lay out one region with flexbox
stages.instructions: Pick one region with multiple items sitting side by side (a nav, a row of tags, a list of links) and lay it out with display: flex, including flex-wrap: wrap and a gap. Resize your browser window narrow enough that the row would otherwise overflow, and confirm it wraps instead.
stages.checkpoint: At least one region uses flexbox with wrap and gap, and visibly wraps onto a second line at a narrow width instead of overflowing.

stages.title: Zoom to 400% and fix what breaks
stages.instructions: Zoom your browser to 400% and check the whole page: does any text get cut off or overlap? Does anything overflow the visible width, forcing horizontal scrolling? Fix any fixed pixel widths you find using max-width and relative sizing instead, and re-check at 400% until nothing is cut off or forces horizontal scroll.
stages.checkpoint: At 400% browser zoom, no text is cut off or overlapping, and nothing forces horizontal scrolling.

rubric.criterion: Selectors are scoped appropriately
rubric.meets: Classes for anything reusable, ids reserved for genuinely unique elements, no unnecessarily broad element selectors overriding unrelated content.

rubric.criterion: The main text passes contrast
rubric.meets: Body text against its background measures at least 4.5:1 on a real contrast checker, not just visual judgment.

rubric.criterion: Padding and margin are used deliberately
rubric.meets: box-sizing: border-box is set, and padding/margin choices reflect an actual understanding of which layer does what.

rubric.criterion: At least one region uses flexbox with wrap
rubric.meets: display: flex, flex-wrap: wrap, and gap are all present and visibly working on a narrow window.

rubric.criterion: The page survives 400% zoom
rubric.meets: No cut-off or overlapping text, and no forced horizontal scrolling at 400% browser zoom.

contentSections.body: A page that survives 400% zoom and passes a real contrast check was designed for how people actually use it — not just for the exact window you happened to be looking at while building it.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions, and earlier ones, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — CSS: Making It Look Right

questions.from: This module — CSS: Making It Look Right
questions.prompt: p { color: black; } and .warning { color: red; } both target the same paragraph. Which wins, and why?

options.label: .warning — a class selector is more specific than an element selector
p — element selectors always take priority
Whichever rule is written last in the file, regardless of selector type

questions.explanation: Specificity, not write order, decides ties between different selector types. A class selector beats a plain element selector regardless of which was written first.

questions.from: This module — CSS: Making It Look Right
questions.prompt: A box has width: 200px and padding: 20px, with the default box-sizing. How wide does it actually render?

options.label: 200px — padding never affects total width
240px — padding is added on top of the content width by default
180px — padding is subtracted from the width

questions.explanation: With the default content-box sizing, width sets only the content layer. Padding (20px on each side) is added on top: 200 + 20 + 20 = 240px total.

questions.from: This module — CSS: Making It Look Right
questions.prompt: What does display: flex, applied to a parent element, do to its direct children by default?

options.label: Arranges them in a horizontal row
Hides them until explicitly shown
Stacks them vertically, same as normal block elements

questions.explanation: display: flex on a parent arranges its direct children into a horizontal row by default — the most common reason to reach for flexbox in the first place.

questions.from: This module — CSS: Making It Look Right
questions.prompt: Why is a red border alone not a sufficient way to mark an invalid form field?

options.label: Red isn't a valid CSS color for borders
Color alone is invisible to anyone who can't reliably distinguish that color difference
Borders can't change color based on validity in CSS

questions.explanation: For someone colorblind, or viewing a dim screen, a color-only signal can fail to register at all. Pairing it with an icon or text ensures the signal survives even when the color difference doesn't.

questions.from: Previous module — HTML: Structure and Meaning
questions.prompt: From HTML: Structure and Meaning: what's wrong with a page built entirely from generic <div>s instead of <header>, <nav>, <main>?

options.label: Nothing, as long as class names describe each div's role
Class names are invisible to screen readers — only real semantic tags are announced as meaningful structure
Divs render more slowly than semantic tags

questions.explanation: A class name exists for CSS/JS to hook into, not for a screen reader to interpret as meaning. Only the actual tag name (nav vs div) carries structural information to assistive technology.

questions.from: Previous module — HTML: Structure and Meaning
questions.prompt: From HTML: Structure and Meaning: what should alt="" (present, empty) be used for?

options.label: A purely decorative image with no content of its own
Any image you haven't gotten around to describing yet
Images that are actually clickable buttons

questions.explanation: alt="" deliberately tells a screen reader to skip an image — correct for pure decoration, wrong for anything informative or functional, which need a real description.

questions.from: Previous module — HTML: Structure and Meaning
questions.prompt: From HTML: Structure and Meaning: why doesn't placeholder text alone count as a label for a form field?

options.label: Placeholder text disappears the moment someone starts typing, and isn't reliably announced by screen readers
Placeholder text is invalid HTML
Placeholder text can only be used on checkboxes

questions.explanation: A real <label>, connected via matching for/id, stays visible and announced regardless of what's typed. Placeholder text vanishes on input and isn't a durable substitute.

questions.from: Previous module — HTML: Structure and Meaning
questions.prompt: From HTML: Structure and Meaning: what does a heading level (h1-h6) describe?

options.label: How large the text should visually appear
The content's rank in the page's outline, independent of visual size
Which page section it links to

questions.explanation: Heading level is structural rank, not a font-size picker — a screen reader user navigates by that outline, which is why levels shouldn't be chosen by how big something should look.

questions.from: Three modules back — Functions
questions.prompt: From Functions: why turn repeated code into a function instead of leaving it copy-pasted in multiple places?

options.label: Functions run faster than repeated code
A change only needs to happen in one place, instead of being kept in sync across every copy
JavaScript requires functions for any code used more than once

questions.explanation: The real benefit is maintenance: one named function means one place to fix a bug or change behavior, instead of hunting down and updating every pasted copy.

questions.from: Four modules back — Making Decisions
questions.prompt: From Making Decisions: what's the risk of deeply nested if/else statements, beyond how they look?

options.label: They run more slowly than flat conditions
It gets easy to lose track of which condition you're actually inside, and to forget a branch entirely
JavaScript limits how many levels of nesting are allowed

questions.explanation: Deep nesting isn't a performance problem — it's a comprehension one. The more levels there are, the easier it is to lose track of the current condition, or to miss a case that needed handling.

title: Finding an element and changing it
description: Before JavaScript can change anything on a page, it has to find the exact element first — the same selector syntax from CSS, now used to grab a real element and change what it says.

learningObjectives.text: Use document.querySelector to find an element by its CSS selector
Change an element's visible text with textContent
Explain why textContent is the safer default over innerHTML for plain text

contentSections.title: document.querySelector finds one thing

contentSections.body:
Your page has `

--

` sitting there as a placeholder. You want a line of JavaScript to fill in today's actual number. Before you can change anything, JavaScript has to find that exact paragraph first — out of everything else on the page.

contentSections.scenario:
The page has `

--

` somewhere in it.
contentSections.question: Which line correctly finds that exact element?

options.label: document.querySelector('#painLevel')
document.querySelector('painLevel')
document.querySelector(painLevel)

feedback.correct: Right. querySelector takes a CSS selector as a string — the same #id syntax you'd write in a stylesheet, quoted, since it's text being passed in, not a variable.
feedback.no_hash: Without the #, this looks for an element whose *tag name* is literally "painlevel" — which doesn't exist — instead of an element with that id. The # is what tells the selector "id," the same as in CSS.
feedback.no_quotes: Without quotes, JavaScript reads painLevel as a variable name, not as text — and unless a variable with that exact name exists, this throws an error before querySelector even runs.

contentSections.concept: document.querySelector(selector) finds the first element matching a CSS selector — #id, .class, or a plain tag name, written exactly like you would in a stylesheet, as a quoted string. It returns the actual element (ready to be changed), or null if nothing matches — which is worth checking for, since JavaScript won't stop you from trying to change a null.

contentSections.body:
```js const painDisplay = document.querySelector('#painLevel'); ``` This stores the actual `

` element in a variable — not its text, the element itself, which you can now read from or change. querySelector reuses exactly the selector syntax from CSS: `'#painLevel'` for an id, `'.warning'` for a class, `'p'` for the first paragraph on the page. If nothing on the page matches, querySelector returns `null` rather than throwing an error — which means a typo in your selector fails silently unless you check for it.
document.querySelector('#id') finds the real element — the same selector syntax as CSS, now handed to JavaScript as a quoted string.

contentSections.title: textContent vs innerHTML, and why one of them is a landmine

contentSections.body: You want to display whatever someone typed into a "notes" field back on the page. Both `.textContent` and `.innerHTML` will technically do it — but one of them will happily turn typed-in text into real, running HTML if that text happens to contain angle brackets, and the other never will.

contentSections.question: If someone typed `` into that field (whether by accident or on purpose), what happens?

options.label: It displays as plain visible text, exactly as typed
innerHTML parses it as real HTML, which can actually execute the embedded script behavior
JavaScript automatically strips out anything that looks like a tag

feedback.plain_text: That's what most people expect, and it's exactly the wrong expectation with innerHTML — .innerHTML parses whatever string it's given as real markup, not as inert text.
feedback.executes: Right. innerHTML parses its input as HTML, tags and all — a typed-in string that happens to look like a working tag gets interpreted as one, which is exactly how this kind of injected content can run.
feedback.auto_strip: There's no automatic stripping — innerHTML has one job (parse this as HTML) and does exactly that, with no built-in judgment about whether the input looks safe.

contentSections.mechanism: `.innerHTML = someString` tells the browser to parse someString as real HTML and insert the result — tags, attributes, and all. `.textContent = someString` inserts it as plain, inert text, no matter what characters are in it; a literal `` typed by a user shows up as the visible text ``, not as an actual image tag. For displaying text someone typed — which is most of what a beginner project does — textContent is both simpler and the safer default.

contentSections.body: Rule of thumb: use `.textContent` when you're inserting plain text (which is almost always, for a beginner project) and reach for `.innerHTML` only when you deliberately mean to insert real markup you trust — your own hardcoded HTML, never text a user typed. `element.style.color = 'red'` is the equivalent pattern for changing a single style property directly from JavaScript, useful for quick, one-off style changes triggered by code.
textContent inserts plain text, always. innerHTML parses its input as real HTML — safe for your own trusted markup, risky for anything a user typed.

title: Events: responding to a click or a keypress
description: addEventListener is how a page stops being static — attaching a function that runs when something specific happens, with the event itself carrying details about exactly what.

learningObjectives.text: Attach a click handler with addEventListener, using the correct three-part structure
Read event.key to distinguish which key was pressed in a keydown handler

contentSections.title: addEventListener needs three things

contentSections.body: You add a button to your symptom tracker meant to log today's entry, but clicking it does absolutely nothing — no error, no output, nothing. The button exists. The problem is nothing on the page is actually listening for the click.

contentSections.scenario:
```html
<button id="logBtn">Log entry</button>
```
and three attempts at making it respond to a click.
contentSections.question: Which of these actually wires up a click handler correctly?

options.label: document.querySelector('#logBtn').addEventListener('click', function() { console.log('logged'); });
document.querySelector('#logBtn').addEventListener(function() { console.log('logged'); });
document.querySelector('#logBtn').click = function() { console.log('logged'); };

feedback.correct: Right. addEventListener takes two arguments: the event type as a string ('click'), and the function to run when it happens.
feedback.missing_type: This is missing the event type string entirely — addEventListener needs to be told *which* event to listen for before it can know when to run the function.
feedback.wrong_property: .click isn't a settable event handler property in the way this suggests — addEventListener is the standard, reliable way to attach a handler, and it supports attaching more than one listener to the same event, which a direct property assignment doesn't.

contentSections.concept: element.addEventListener(eventType, callback) attaches a function that runs whenever that event happens on that element. 'click' is the most common event type; the callback is an ordinary function containing whatever code should run in response. Nothing happens until this line runs — a button with no listener attached is just a shape that happens to be clickable, doing nothing when clicked.

contentSections.body: addEventListener(eventType, callback) — the event type as a quoted string, then the function to run when it happens.

contentSections.title: The event object tells you what happened

contentSections.body: You want someone to be able to press Enter in a symptom-log text field instead of always having to click a separate Save button — genuinely useful if clicking a small target is hard on a given day. That means listening for a keypress and checking specifically which key it was.

contentSections.hint: The event object that's automatically passed into the callback carries details about what actually happened — including, for a keyboard event, which key.
contentSections.answer: 'Enter' — a string naming the specific key. Every keyboard event automatically comes with an event object as the callback's first argument, and event.key tells you which key was involved: 'Enter', 'a', 'Escape', ' ' (space), and so on. This is what lets you write `if (event.key === 'Enter') { ... }` inside the handler to run code only for that one specific key, while still catching every keypress in general.

contentSections.body: The callback function passed to addEventListener automatically receives an **event object** as its first argument — conventionally named `event` or `e` — carrying details specific to what happened. For a `'click'` event that's things like which element was clicked; for a `'keydown'` event, `event.key` is the specific key pressed. Checking `event.key === 'Enter'` inside a keydown handler is exactly how you'd let someone submit a form by pressing Enter, without requiring a mouse click at all.
The event object passed into every handler carries the specifics — event.key for which key was pressed, checked with a plain ===.

title: Reading what someone typed into a form
description: An input's .value holds whatever's currently typed into it, as a string — and a submit event's default page reload is exactly the thing that erases it before you can read it, unless you stop that reload on purpose.

learningObjectives.text: Read a form field's current value with .value
Convert a numeric input's .value to a real number before doing arithmetic
Use event.preventDefault() to stop a form's default page reload on submit

contentSections.title: input.value holds the current text

contentSections.body: You've got `<input type="number" id="painLevel">` in your symptom log form. Someone types 6. What line of code actually reaches into that field and gets the 6 out, so you can use it?

contentSections.scenario:
```html
<input type="number" id="painLevel">
```
someone has typed 6 into.
contentSections.question: Which of these correctly reads what's currently in the field?

options.label: document.querySelector('#painLevel').value
document.querySelector('#painLevel').textContent
document.querySelector('#painLevel')

feedback.value: Right. .value is the property that holds a form field's current content — what's actually typed in, right now, as a string.
feedback.textcontent:
.textContent is for reading or setting the text *inside* an element like a

or

— an 's typed content lives in a completely separate property, .value, not in textContent.
feedback.element_only: This gets you the input element itself — the whole object representing the field — not what's currently typed into it. You'd need .value on top of this to get the actual 6.

contentSections.concept: An <input>'s current content lives in its .value property, always as a string — even for type="number", where you might expect a real number back. `document.querySelector('#painLevel').value` reading 6 out of the field actually gives you the string "6", not the number 6.

contentSections.body: An input's .value is always a string — even for a number field. Convert it with Number(...) before doing arithmetic on it.

contentSections.title: Preventing the page from reloading when a form submits

contentSections.body: You write a submit handler that logs the form's value to the console — and the moment someone clicks Submit, the whole page flashes and reloads, wiping out whatever you were about to see. The form did exactly what forms do by default: submitted itself, which means reloading the page.

contentSections.question: The console.log briefly flashes, if you catch it at all, and then the page reloads and the log is gone. What's missing?

options.label: event.preventDefault(), to stop the form's default page-reload behavior
The console.log line is written wrong
Nothing — this is just how forms always work and can't be changed

feedback.prevent_default: Right. A form's default behavior on submit is to actually submit itself — normally sending data to a server and reloading the page in the process. Nothing here stops that default behavior from happening.
feedback.log_wrong: The console.log line is written correctly — the problem isn't what it says, it's that the page reloads before you have any real chance to see the output, wiping the console along with it.
feedback.unfixable: This default behavior is genuinely, deliberately overridable — event.preventDefault() exists specifically for this, which is exactly why forms with JavaScript-driven submission are possible at all.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is one line, called first inside the handler: `event.preventDefault();`. This tells the browser "don't do your default thing for this event" — for a submit event, that default thing is the page reload. With it in place, the rest of your handler runs normally, and the page stays exactly where it is.

contentSections.body: A form reloads the page on submit by default. event.preventDefault(), called first inside the handler, is what stops that.

title: Showing and hiding without breaking screen readers
description: Toggling a section's visibility with CSS is only half the job — without also updating an aria attribute, a sighted user sees the state change and a screen reader user gets no signal that anything happened at all.

learningObjectives.text: Use classList.toggle to show or hide a section by adding or removing a CSS class
Explain why a purely visual show/hide leaves screen reader users without a state signal
Update aria-expanded alongside a visibility toggle

contentSections.title: display: none actually removes it, for everyone

contentSections.body: A "Show details" button on your symptom log toggles a hidden panel of extra notes. You could hide that panel with CSS in more than one way — and only one of them actually removes it from a screen reader's path, rather than just making it invisible to the eye while still technically "there."

contentSections.scenario: Three ways to hide a details panel: display: none;, opacity: 0;, and visibility: hidden;.
contentSections.question: Which of these is actually removed from both the visual page and a screen reader's reading order?

options.label: display: none;
opacity: 0;
None of them — CSS visibility never affects screen readers

feedback.display_none: Right. display: none removes the element from the layout entirely and takes it out of the accessibility tree — a screen reader skips it completely, matching what a sighted user sees.
feedback.opacity: opacity: 0 makes the element invisible to the eye, but it's still fully present in the layout and still reachable by keyboard Tab and a screen reader — someone can end up focused on, or hearing about, content they can't see at all, which is arguably worse than not hiding it.
feedback.none_affect: CSS visibility genuinely does affect what a screen reader announces — display: none is specifically excluded from the accessibility tree, which is exactly why it's the right tool for actually hiding something.

contentSections.concept: display: none removes an element from the rendered layout and the accessibility tree together — hidden for everyone, consistently. opacity: 0 (and, differently, visibility: hidden for keyboard reachability) only affects visual appearance, leaving the element still technically present and sometimes still reachable — a mismatch between what's seen and what's exposed to assistive technology.

contentSections.body: display: none removes an element for everyone, consistently. opacity and some other visual tricks only fool the eye, leaving it reachable to keyboard and screen reader.

contentSections.title: Telling assistive tech state changed too

contentSections.body: The "Show details" button toggles the panel correctly now — display: none comes and goes exactly as intended. But the button itself still just says "Show details" either way, and nothing announces to a screen reader user whether the panel they can't currently see is now open or still closed.

contentSections.scenario: A toggle button correctly shows/hides a panel using classList.toggle and display: none.
contentSections.question: Which of these actually communicate the button's current state to a screen reader user, beyond the panel's own visibility?

items.label: Setting aria-expanded="true"/"false" on the button, updated on every toggle
Changing the button's own text between "Show details" and "Hide details"
Relying on the panel's own appearance/disappearance as the only signal
Changing the button's background color when expanded, with nothing else

explanation.aria_expanded: This is the standard, purpose-built signal — a screen reader announces "expanded" or "collapsed" for a control with aria-expanded set, directly telling the user the current state without needing to separately check the panel.
explanation.button_text: A genuinely helpful, low-tech signal too — changing the label itself communicates state to everyone, sighted or not, with no special attribute required.
explanation.visual_only: The panel's own appearance is exactly the thing a screen reader user isn't perceiving visually — relying on it alone as the state signal leaves them with nothing.
explanation.color_change: A color change alone repeats the color-only-signal mistake from the CSS module — invisible to a screen reader, and unreliable for anyone who can't distinguish the specific color shift.

contentSections.synthesis: The strongest real fix combines both working signals: update aria-expanded on the button so a screen reader announces the state directly, and change the button's own visible text so everyone gets the same information, not just people who can see the panel appear or disappear.

contentSections.body: A visual-only toggle leaves screen reader users with no signal at all. aria-expanded, updated alongside the visibility toggle, closes that gap.

title: Keeping the page usable by keyboard
description: A <div> styled to look exactly like a button is invisible to the Tab key — native interactive elements come with keyboard behavior built in for free, and reproducing it by hand is easy to get wrong.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a <div> with a click handler isn't reachable by keyboard Tab, unlike a real <button>
Test a page's interactive elements using only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter and Space
Recognize outline: none with no replacement as a genuine accessibility failure

contentSections.title: Tab order follows the HTML, not the CSS

contentSections.body:
A designer wanted a very specifically styled "Log entry" button, and it got built as `
Log entry
` — styled with CSS to look absolutely identical to a real button. It works fine with a mouse. Someone navigating by keyboard alone, tabbing through the page, skips right past it — it's never reachable at all.

contentSections.scenario:
```html
Log entry
``` styled with CSS to look identical to a real button, but never receives keyboard focus when pressing Tab.
contentSections.question: Why doesn't pressing Tab ever land on this div, the way it would on a real <button>?

options.label: A <div> was never designed to be part of the keyboard tab order at all — that's built into <button>, <a>, and <input> by default, not into <div>
The CSS styling is somehow blocking keyboard access
onclick handlers disable keyboard access

feedback.not_focusable: Right. Real interactive elements — <button>, <a href="...">, <input> — are built to be part of the keyboard tab order automatically. A <div> is not, no matter how it's styled or what click handler it has.
feedback.css_blocks: Styling something to look like a button doesn't touch its underlying focusability at all — CSS controls appearance, not whether an element is part of the tab order.
feedback.onclick_disables: onclick works fine for a mouse click regardless of the element — the missing piece isn't the click handler, it's that a div was never keyboard-focusable to begin with, click handler or not.

contentSections.mechanism: Browsers give native interactive elements — <button>, <a>, <input>, <select> — keyboard behavior for free: they're reachable by Tab, and pressing Enter (or Space, for buttons) activates them, all without a single line of extra JavaScript. A <div> or <span> gets none of that automatically. Reproducing it by hand means adding tabindex="0" and writing your own keydown handler for Enter and Space — genuinely possible, but extra work to correctly recreate something a real <button> already does for free.

contentSections.body: The fix in almost every real case is the simplest possible one: use `<button>` instead of a styled `<div>`. CSS can restyle a real `<button>` to look like absolutely anything — there's no visual limitation that forces reaching for a div — while keeping all of its free keyboard behavior. This is the same lesson as the HTML module's semantic-elements pod, applied specifically to interactivity: the native element already does the hard part.
<button> is keyboard-accessible for free. A styled <div> is not, no matter how convincingly it looks like a button.

contentSections.title: Testing it yourself: unplug the mouse

contentSections.body: The cheapest, most honest accessibility test for anything you build in this module: put the mouse aside entirely, and try to complete the whole interaction using only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, and Space. If you get stuck anywhere, that's exactly where a keyboard-only user would get stuck too.

contentSections.scenario: You're keyboard-testing a symptom log page: a text input, a "Log entry" button, and a "Show details" toggle.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuine passes of a keyboard-only test?

items.label: Tab reaches every interactive element on the page, in a sensible order
Pressing Enter while focused on the button actually triggers it, same as clicking
A visible focus outline shows exactly which element currently has focus
A dropdown that only opens when hovered with a mouse, with no keyboard equivalent

explanation.tab_reaches_all: This is the baseline — if Tab silently skips an interactive element, it's unreachable by keyboard, full stop, regardless of anything else about it.
explanation.enter_activates: Reaching an element with Tab isn't enough on its own — it also has to actually respond to Enter (or Space) the way a click would, or reaching it accomplishes nothing.
explanation.visible_focus: Without a visible focus indicator, a keyboard user can technically be "on" an element with zero way to see where they currently are on the page — this is exactly what CSS's `outline: none`, applied without a real replacement, breaks.
explanation.mouse_only_hover: A hover-only interaction has no keyboard equivalent at all — Tab can reach the element, but nothing a keyboard user can do triggers the same behavior a mouse hover does.

contentSections.synthesis: All four matter together: reachable by Tab, activatable by Enter/Space, visibly showing where focus currently is, and never gated behind mouse-only interactions like hover. Missing any one of them breaks the keyboard-only path even if the other three are perfect.

contentSections.body: One specific trap worth calling out by name: `outline: none;` (or `outline: 0;`) removes the default focus ring some developers find visually unappealing — and if nothing replaces it, keyboard users lose the only visible signal of where they are on the page entirely. If you don't like the default outline's look, replace it with your own visible focus style (a custom outline, a background change) — never remove it and leave nothing in its place.
Unplug the mouse and try your own page with just Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter and Space. Wherever you get stuck is exactly where a keyboard-only user gets stuck.

title: Practice — Wire Up Eight Interactions

learningObjectives.text: Apply querySelector, addEventListener, .value and accessibility-preserving toggling to small stated requirements

contentSections.title: Eight interactions, the same handful of rules

contentSections.body: Every one of these traces back to something from this module: finding the right element, attaching a listener correctly, reading .value and converting it, stopping a form's default reload, and keeping a show/hide toggle usable by keyboard and screen reader both.
Almost every interaction bug in this module comes down to one question: did I find the right element, listen for the right event, and keep it usable without a mouse?

title: Lab — Make Your Page Interactive

learningObjectives.text: Wire a real interaction end to end: find, listen, read, update
Handle a form submission without a page reload
Verify a whole interactive flow using only the keyboard

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This is the page from the last two labs, getting its first real behavior: something a visitor can actually type into, click, or toggle, that changes what's on the page in response — built with real elements, tested with the mouse put aside.

contentSections.title: Make your page interactive
contentSections.brief: Using the page you've built and styled in the last two modules' labs, add a real interaction: a form that reads what someone typed and displays it back without reloading the page, plus a show/hide toggle that stays correct for both a mouse and a screen reader.
contentSections.deliverable: An interactive page that works fully by keyboard alone.

stages.title: Find and read
stages.instructions: Add a small form with at least one real <input> and a <label> connected to it (reusing lesson 5's rules from the HTML module). Write JavaScript that finds the input with querySelector and can read its current .value — console.log it for now to confirm you're getting the right value.
stages.checkpoint: querySelector correctly finds the input, and its .value logs the right typed content to the console.

stages.title: Handle the submit without reloading
stages.instructions: Attach a submit listener to the form. Call event.preventDefault() first thing inside it. Read the input's value (converting to a number with Number(...) if it's meant to be numeric), and use textContent to display it somewhere else on the page — a real, working display, not just a console.log.
stages.checkpoint: Submitting the form updates the page's displayed text and does not reload the page.

stages.title: A show/hide toggle that stays correct for everyone
stages.instructions: Add a button that toggles a section of the page (display: none via classList.toggle), updating both aria-expanded on the button and the button's own visible text to reflect the current state, following lesson 4's pattern exactly.
stages.checkpoint: The toggle button's aria-expanded value and its visible text both correctly reflect whether the section is currently shown or hidden.

stages.title: Unplug the mouse
stages.instructions: Put the mouse aside and complete the entire flow — typing into the field, submitting the form, toggling the section — using only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, and Space. If any real <button> or interactive element is unreachable, or if focus is ever invisible, fix it before calling this done.
stages.checkpoint: The complete interaction — typing, submitting, toggling — works start to finish using only the keyboard, with focus visible at every step.

rubric.criterion: The element is found and read correctly
rubric.meets: querySelector locates the right element, and .value is read (and converted with Number(...) if numeric) correctly.

rubric.criterion: The form submits without reloading the page
rubric.meets: event.preventDefault() is called, and the page's own state updates in place instead of refreshing.

rubric.criterion: The displayed result uses textContent, not innerHTML
rubric.meets: Any user-originated text is inserted with textContent, not innerHTML, unless there's a specific, deliberate reason otherwise.

rubric.criterion: The toggle stays correct for assistive technology
rubric.meets: aria-expanded and the button's own text both update correctly alongside the visual toggle.

rubric.criterion: The whole flow works by keyboard alone
rubric.meets: Every interactive step — type, submit, toggle — is reachable and operable using only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter and Space, with focus always visible.

contentSections.body: An interaction that only works with a mouse isn't finished — it's finished when it survives being unplugged from one.

options.label: textContent runs faster
innerHTML parses its input as real HTML, so typed-in tag-like text can be interpreted as actual markup
innerHTML only works on <div> elements

options.label: A real number, automatically
A string, even though the field only accepts numeric input

onclick doesn't work on divs at all
