title: Storing something in the browser
description: localStorage is a small key-value store built into every browser, saved across reloads and browser restarts — but it only ever stores strings, no matter what you hand it.

learningObjectives.text: Save and retrieve a value with localStorage.setItem/getItem
Distinguish localStorage's persistence from sessionStorage's tab-scoped lifetime
Explain why a value retrieved from localStorage is always a string

contentSections.title: localStorage: a tiny key-value store built into the browser

contentSections.body: You type a note into your symptom tracker, refresh the page by accident, and it's gone — every reload starts from nothing, because up to now, nothing about this track has saved anything anywhere. The browser itself has a small built-in place to fix exactly that, with no server needed at all.

contentSections.scenario: You want to save the text "Feeling steadier today" under the name "latestNote", so it's still there after a page reload.
contentSections.question: Which line actually saves it to the browser's persistent storage?

options.label: localStorage.setItem('latestNote', 'Feeling steadier today');
let latestNote = 'Feeling steadier today';
localStorage.latestNote = 'Feeling steadier today';

feedback.correct: Right. localStorage.setItem(key, value) is the actual method for saving a value under a name, and it persists across reloads and even closing the browser entirely.
feedback.variable: An ordinary variable lives only in memory for as long as the page stays open — the moment the page reloads, every variable is wiped and recreated from scratch, saving nothing.
feedback.dot_access: This can appear to work in some cases, but setItem is the real, standard, reliable method — dot-property assignment on localStorage isn't the documented, guaranteed way to store a value and can behave inconsistently.

contentSections.concept: localStorage.setItem(key, value) saves a value under a name (the key), persisting it across page reloads and even full browser restarts, tied to that specific website. localStorage.getItem(key) retrieves it later. Unlike a regular variable — which is wiped the instant the page reloads — localStorage genuinely sticks around until something explicitly clears it.

contentSections.body: localStorage.setItem/getItem persists across reloads and browser restarts — a plain variable is wiped the instant the page reloads.

contentSections.title: Everything stored is a string, always

contentSections.body: You save today's pain level with `localStorage.setItem('painLevel', 6)`, reload the page, read it back, and add 1 to show tomorrow's projected value — and get "61" instead of 7. This is the exact same trap from way back in the track, wearing a new outfit.

contentSections.question: This prints "61", not 7. Why?

options.label: localStorage always converts its stored value to a string, so saved is the string "6", and + joins it with 1 as text
There's a typo in setItem
+ never works with localStorage values

feedback.always_string: Right. Even though 6 was passed in as a real number, localStorage converts everything to a string before storing it — getItem always hands back a string, and "6" + 1 joins as text rather than adding.
feedback.typo: There's no typo — the code runs exactly as written. The surprise is in what localStorage does to the type of the value, not in a spelling mistake.
feedback.never_works: + works fine here — it's doing exactly what + does with a string on one side: joining as text. The issue is the type of the retrieved value, not the operator failing.

contentSections.mechanism: localStorage can only ever store strings — if you pass it a number, it silently converts that number to its string form before saving. getItem always returns a string back (or null if nothing was saved under that key), regardless of what type went in. Anything you plan to do arithmetic with has to be converted deliberately with Number(...) after reading it back, exactly like every other string-that-should-be-a-number situation in this track.

contentSections.body: localStorage only ever stores and returns strings — even a number you saved comes back as text, needing Number(...) before real arithmetic.

title: JSON: the shape data travels in
description: localStorage only stores strings — but real data is usually more than one value at a time. JSON is the text format that lets a whole object or array travel as a single string and come back out intact.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why saving an object directly with setItem produces "[object Object]" instead of real data
Convert an object or array to a JSON string with JSON.stringify
Convert a JSON string back into a real, usable object or array with JSON.parse

contentSections.title: JSON looks like an object, but it's actually text

contentSections.body: A single symptom log entry isn't one value — it's several together: a date, a pain level, some notes. You try to save the whole thing at once with `localStorage.setItem('entry', { date: '2026-08-08', pain: 6 })`, read it back later, and get the oddly useless string "[object Object]" instead of your actual data.

contentSections.question: What's actually happening here?

options.label: setItem converts anything that isn't already a string to text by calling a generic, unhelpful conversion — objects become the literal text "[object Object]"
localStorage rejected the object and saved nothing
This is a typo in the property names

feedback.generic_convert: Right. Since localStorage can only store strings, it converts whatever you give it — for a plain object, that generic conversion produces the unhelpful literal text "[object Object]", with all the actual data (date, pain) discarded in the process.
feedback.rejected: It didn't reject anything — getItem does return a real string, "[object Object]", it's just not the data you wanted. Something was saved; it's just the wrong something.
feedback.typo: The object's properties are written correctly — this isn't about spelling, it's about what happens when an object is handed to something that can only store text.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is converting the object to a real, data-preserving string first — not the generic "[object Object]" conversion, but JSON: `JSON.stringify(entry)` produces `'{"date":"2026-08-08","pain":6}'`, a string that actually contains all the original data, in a standard text format that can be turned back into a real object later.

contentSections.body: **JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format for representing structured data — objects and arrays — as a string. It looks almost identical to a JavaScript object literal, but it's genuinely just text: `'{"date":"2026-08-08","pain":6}'` is a string, not a real object with a `.pain` property you could access yet. `JSON.stringify(value)` converts a real JavaScript object or array into its JSON string form — this is what actually preserves the data, unlike the generic "[object Object]" conversion.
JSON.stringify converts a real object or array into a text string that actually preserves the data — the default string conversion doesn't.

contentSections.title: JSON.parse turns the text back into real data

contentSections.body: You've correctly saved `JSON.stringify(entry)` to localStorage. You read it back with getItem — and it's still just a string. You can't do `.pain` on a string; you need the actual object back, not its text form.

contentSections.hint: JSON.parse is the reverse of JSON.stringify — text in, a real, usable object out.
contentSections.answer: 6 (the real number, not a string) — JSON.parse takes a JSON-formatted string and rebuilds it into an actual JavaScript object, with real properties you can dot-access, and with the correct types restored (6 was a number in the original JSON, so it's a number again after parsing, not text). stringify and parse are exact inverses: object → string with stringify, string → object with parse.

contentSections.body: JSON.stringify turns real data into a saveable string. JSON.parse turns that string back into real, usable data — always used as a pair.

title: Loading saved data and handling none being there
description: The very first time anyone visits your page, there's nothing saved yet — getItem returns null, and code that doesn't plan for that crashes on the first visit, every single time, for every new visitor.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what getItem returns when nothing has been saved under that key
Diagnose a crash caused by using a null value as if it were real data
Write a safe load pattern that falls back to a sensible default when nothing is saved

contentSections.title: The first time ever, there's nothing saved yet

contentSections.body: You test your symptom log on your own browser, where you've already saved a few entries — it loads and displays perfectly. You send the link to a friend, who's never opened the page before, and it crashes immediately, before they can do anything at all.

contentSections.question: Why does this crash for a first-time visitor, when it works fine for you?

options.label: getItem returns null when nothing's saved; JSON.parse(null) itself doesn't error, but the result is null, and null.length crashes
localStorage doesn't work for new visitors
JSON.parse always requires at least one prior save to function

feedback.null_chain: Right. getItem returns null for a key that's never been saved. JSON.parse(null) actually returns null too, without throwing — but the very next line, entries.length, tries to read .length off of null, which does throw, crashing the page.
feedback.doesnt_work: localStorage works identically for every visitor — the difference is purely about whether they have any prior saved data under this key, not whether the feature itself works for them.
feedback.requires_prior: JSON.parse works on any valid JSON string, first-time visitor or not — the actual problem is what happens one line later, using the result as if it were guaranteed to be a real array.

contentSections.mechanism: getItem(key) returns null, not an error and not an empty string, when nothing has ever been saved under that key. Code that treats the result as if it's guaranteed to be real data — assuming it can always be parsed, or that it always has a .length — crashes the instant it meets a visitor (or a browser, or a cleared cache) with genuinely nothing saved yet. This is invisible during your own testing precisely because you already have data sitting there from earlier testing.

contentSections.body: This matters because "works when I test it" and "works for a first-time visitor" are two different claims — your own browser almost always has leftover saved data from earlier testing, silently hiding this exact bug until someone with a genuinely clean browser hits it. Checking for a first-time (empty) state isn't an edge case to handle eventually — for storage code, it's the very first thing that will actually happen to a real new visitor.
getItem returns null for a never-saved key — treating that null as if it were real data is exactly what crashes on a genuinely new visitor.

contentSections.title: A safe load pattern

contentSections.body: The fix isn't complicated once you know to look for it — one line that checks whether anything was actually saved, and falls back to a sensible starting value (an empty list, in this case) if not, before ever trying to parse or use it.

contentSections.intro: You're writing a safe load function for a list of symptom entries, defaulting to an empty list on a first visit.

fields.prompt: First, read whatever's currently saved under the key 'entries'
fields.feedback: getItem(key) is the correct, reliable way to read a saved value — it may come back null, which the next step needs to handle.

fields.prompt: Before parsing, check whether anything was actually saved
fields.feedback: saved ? JSON.parse(saved) : [] only calls JSON.parse when saved is truthy (a real, non-null string) — otherwise it falls back directly to an empty array, safely skipping the crash entirely.

fields.prompt: Now that entries is guaranteed to be a real array either way, what can the rest of the code safely assume?
options: entries.length and other array operations are always safe to use, even on a brand-new visitor's first load
entries might still be null sometimes
entries needs a second null check before every use
fields.correctValue: entries.length and other array operations are always safe to use, even on a brand-new visitor's first load
fields.feedback: Because the fallback guarantees entries is always a real array — empty or full — every line after this can treat it as safe, real data, with no repeated null-checking scattered throughout the rest of the code.

contentSections.body: This same pattern generalizes beyond arrays: `saved ? JSON.parse(saved) : someDefault` works for a default empty object (`{}`), a default settings object with sensible starting values, or anything else. The core idea is always the same — decide, in one place, what "nothing's been saved yet" should mean for your specific data, and let everything downstream trust that a real, usable value always exists.
Check for null and fall back to a sensible default in one place — then everything downstream can trust the data is real, without repeated null checks.

title: What should never go in browser storage
description: localStorage has no encryption and no password — anyone with access to the device (or its devtools) can read every byte of it in plain text, which makes some kinds of data genuinely unsafe to put there at all.

learningObjectives.text: Explain that localStorage is readable, unencrypted plain text to anyone with device access
Judge which kinds of data are safe versus unsafe to store client-side
Recognize that localStorage is not a durable backup and can be cleared without warning

contentSections.title: Anyone with access to this browser can read it in plain text

contentSections.body: You store someone's account password in localStorage "just to keep them logged in." Open the browser's developer tools on that exact device — no special hacking skill required, just the built-in tools every browser ships with — and that password is sitting there, in plain readable text, for anyone with physical access to the device to see.

contentSections.scenario: A health-tracking app is deciding what's safe to keep in localStorage versus what needs to live on a real, authenticated server instead.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuinely risky to store in localStorage, given that it's unencrypted and readable by anyone with device access?

items.label: A plaintext account password
A full medical record with the person's name and diagnosis history
Whether the user prefers dark mode
An unsent draft of a note the person is still writing, not yet submitted anywhere

explanation.password: Genuinely risky — a password stored in plain, readable localStorage is one shared or stolen device away from being fully exposed, with no encryption standing in the way.
explanation.full_record: Also genuinely risky — an identifiable full medical record is exactly the kind of sensitive, regulated data that needs to live behind real authentication on a real server, not in a client-side store anyone with the device can open.
explanation.theme_pref: Low-stakes — knowing someone prefers dark mode reveals essentially nothing sensitive if someone else reads it.
explanation.draft_note: Also reasonably low-stakes on its own — an unsent draft is exactly the kind of convenience data localStorage is good for, as long as its actual content isn't itself sensitive.

contentSections.synthesis: The dividing line isn't "is this data" — it's "would it be a real problem if anyone with access to this device could read it in plain text, right now, with the browser's own built-in tools." Preferences and drafts: usually fine. Credentials and identifiable sensitive records: never, without real encryption and authentication a browser's built-in storage doesn't provide.

contentSections.body: localStorage's only real protection is same-origin scoping — a different website can't read another site's localStorage. That's it. It has no encryption, no password, and nothing stopping anyone who can open the browser's developer tools on that device from reading every key and value directly. Anything that would be a real problem if someone else saw it — passwords, full names paired with sensitive health details, anything you'd call "private" in the everyday sense — needs to go through a real, authenticated backend, which is a later module's territory, not client-side storage.
localStorage is plain, unencrypted text, readable by anyone with access to the device. Never store a password or identifiable sensitive data in it.

contentSections.title: Storage also isn't guaranteed to stick around

contentSections.body: Someone uses your symptom tracker in a private/incognito browser window for a week, logging real entries the whole time — then closes that window, and every single entry is gone, permanently, with no warning and no way to recover it.

contentSections.question: What happens to localStorage saved during a private/incognito browsing session, once that private window is closed?
contentSections.hint: Private browsing is specifically designed to leave nothing behind once the session ends — that includes more than just browsing history.
contentSections.answer: It's wiped, completely and permanently, the moment the private window closes — that's the entire point of private browsing mode. More generally, localStorage can also be cleared by the user manually clearing site data, by browser settings that limit storage duration, or by the browser itself reclaiming space under storage pressure. None of this counts as a malfunction — localStorage was never designed as a guaranteed, permanent backup, and treating it as the only copy of something someone would be upset to lose is a real design mistake, not a hypothetical one.

contentSections.body: For anything that genuinely matters if it's lost — more than a few days of real tracked data, something someone would be upset to lose — the honest answer is that client-side storage alone isn't enough; it needs a real backend save (a later module) as the durable copy, with localStorage at most as a fast, convenient cache on top of that. For low-stakes convenience data (a draft, a preference), losing it occasionally is a fine trade-off for the simplicity of not needing a server at all.
localStorage can be wiped by private browsing, manual clearing, or browser storage limits — it's convenient, not a backup.

title: Data that survives a corrupted save
description: A save that gets cut off partway through — a crash, a full disk, a closed tab mid-write — leaves behind a string that isn't valid JSON anymore, and JSON.parse doesn't fail quietly when that happens.

learningObjectives.text: Explain that JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError on invalid JSON rather than returning null
Diagnose a whole-page crash caused by an unguarded JSON.parse on corrupted data
Wrap a risky parse in try/catch with a sensible fallback instead of a crash

contentSections.title: JSON.parse throws when the string isn't valid JSON

contentSections.body: A save gets interrupted — a browser tab closes mid-write, a device runs out of storage space partway through — and what's left in localStorage is a truncated, broken fragment: `'{"date":"2026-08-08","pai'`, cut off mid-word. The next time the page loads, it doesn't just show empty data. It crashes completely, before anything else on the page can even render.

contentSections.question: This has the safe null-check pattern from lesson 3 already. Why does it still crash on a corrupted (but non-null) saved string?

options.label: JSON.parse throws a real error — a SyntaxError — when given text that isn't valid JSON, and nothing here catches that error
The null check from lesson 3 doesn't actually work
localStorage automatically fixes corrupted strings before returning them

feedback.throws_uncaught: Right. The lesson 3 pattern correctly handles "nothing was saved" (null), but a corrupted, non-null string is a different problem entirely — JSON.parse throws a genuine SyntaxError on malformed JSON, and an uncaught error stops the rest of the script from running, taking down the whole page with it.
feedback.null_check_broken: The null check works exactly as designed — the saved value here isn't null at all, it's a real (but broken) string, which is precisely why the null check doesn't catch this different kind of problem.
feedback.auto_fix: localStorage does no validation or repair at all — it stores and returns exactly whatever string it was given, corrupted or not, with zero attempt to fix anything.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Checking for null (lesson 3) and handling a parse failure (this lesson) are two separate problems with two separate fixes. The fix here is wrapping the parse itself in a try/catch block, so a SyntaxError gets caught and handled deliberately, instead of crashing the entire script.

contentSections.body: `JSON.parse(validJsonString)` returns real data. `JSON.parse(invalidString)` doesn't return null or an empty result — it **throws**, meaning it stops execution right there with an error, unless something is specifically set up to catch it. This is different behavior from most of what's shown up in this track so far, where a wrong result quietly appears instead of stopping the program — here, a genuinely broken input actively halts everything after it.
JSON.parse throws a real error on invalid JSON — it doesn't fail quietly the way most type mismatches in this track have so far.

contentSections.title: Falling back to something reasonable, not a blank crash

contentSections.body: The fix isn't to prevent corruption — a mid-write interruption can happen no matter how carefully the saving code is written. The fix is making sure that when it does happen, the page recovers gracefully instead of dying completely.

contentSections.scenario: Handling a possibly-corrupted saved string when loading the page.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuinely part of a graceful recovery from corrupted saved data?

items.label: Wrapping JSON.parse in try/catch, falling back to an empty array in the catch block
Letting the user know their saved data couldn't be read, rather than silently vanishing with no explanation
Doing nothing and letting the uncaught error crash the whole page
Assuming saved JSON is always valid, since it was your own code that saved it

explanation.try_catch: This is the core fix — a caught error means the rest of the page can keep running, recovering into a known, safe state (an empty list) instead of dying entirely.
explanation.user_message: A real improvement beyond the bare minimum — telling someone their previous data couldn't be loaded, rather than just silently starting them over with no explanation, respects that they might notice something's missing and wonder why.
explanation.ignore_error: This is exactly the current, broken behavior — an uncaught SyntaxError takes the entire script down with it, not just the one feature that was loading data.
explanation.assume_valid: "My own code saved it, so it must be fine" ignores every real cause of corruption — a crash mid-write, a full disk, a browser killed at the wrong moment — none of which have anything to do with whether the saving code itself was correct.

contentSections.synthesis: try/catch turns "the whole page crashes because of one bad string" into "this one feature quietly recovers, and the user finds out what happened" — a small amount of defensive code standing between a rare but real failure and a genuinely broken page.

contentSections.body: try/catch around JSON.parse turns a corrupted save from a full page crash into a quiet, deliberate recovery.

title: What an API is, without the jargon
description: An API is an agreed-upon way to ask another program for data and get a real, structured answer back — closer to ordering off a menu than to walking into someone else's kitchen.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what an API is in concrete terms, without relying on the acronym
Distinguish using a real API from scraping or directly manipulating another site's page
Explain what an endpoint is and why picking the wrong one gets the wrong data, not an error

contentSections.title: A menu, not a mystery

contentSections.body: You want today's actual weather shown on your page — not typed in by hand, the real current temperature. You have no idea how a weather service's servers work internally, what database they use, or how they collect the data. You don't need to. You need one specific, agreed-upon way to ask them for it.

contentSections.scenario: Three ways someone might try to get another service's weather data onto their own page.
contentSections.question: Which of these is what "using an API" actually means?

options.label: Sending a request to a URL the weather service specifically publishes for this purpose, and getting back structured data in response
Copy-pasting the weather service's own displayed numbers into your page by hand every morning
Writing code that opens the weather website and tries to scrape numbers out of its visual page layout

feedback.real_api: Right. An API is a deliberate, published way for one program to ask another for data — a specific URL you're meant to request, returning a specific, structured answer meant to be read by code, not by a human's eyes.
feedback.manual_copy: This works, technically, but it's not automated and not an API — it's manual labor standing in for what an API is actually built to do automatically.
feedback.scraping: Scraping reads a page built for humans to look at, not for programs to parse — it breaks the moment that page's visual layout changes even slightly, since nothing about it was designed to be machine-readable in the first place.

contentSections.concept: An API (Application Programming Interface) is a defined, published way for one program to ask another program for data or action, and get a predictable, structured response back — think of it like a restaurant menu: you don't need to know how the kitchen works, you just need to know what you're allowed to order and what you'll get back. A weather service's API is built specifically to be requested by code; its regular website is built to be looked at by a person.

contentSections.body: Most APIs on the modern web respond with **JSON** — the exact same text format from the storing-data module, just arriving over the network instead of coming out of localStorage. That's not a coincidence: JSON became the standard shape for structured data to travel in, whether it's traveling into browser storage or across the internet from another service.
An API is a published, deliberate way to ask another program for data — built for code to request, unlike a regular webpage built for a person to look at.

contentSections.title: Endpoints: one API, many specific questions

contentSections.body: A weather API doesn't have just one URL — it might have one for "today's weather in a specific city," a completely different one for "the five-day forecast," and another for "weather alerts." Request the wrong one and you don't get an error — you get real, valid data, just not the data you actually wanted.

contentSections.scenario: A weather API publishes two URLs: /current?city=Boston (today's conditions) and /forecast?city=Boston (the next five days). A developer wants today's temperature and requests /forecast?city=Boston by mistake.
contentSections.question: What actually happens?

options.label: A real, valid response comes back — just five days of forecast data instead of today's current conditions
The API rejects the request with an error, since it's not what was intended
Both endpoints always return identical data regardless of which is requested

feedback.wrong_data: Right. The API has no way to know what the developer actually meant to ask for — it correctly answers the exact question that was actually sent, which in this case just isn't the question the developer intended.
feedback.rejects: There's nothing invalid about requesting /forecast — it's a real, working endpoint. The mistake is in which one was chosen, not in how the request was formed.
feedback.identical: Different endpoints exist specifically because they return different things — that's the entire reason an API publishes more than one of them.

contentSections.mechanism: An **endpoint** is one specific URL within an API, built to answer one specific kind of question. Picking the wrong endpoint is a silent bug, not a loud one — you get real, structurally valid data back, just not the data you meant to ask for, which can be genuinely harder to notice than an outright error. Reading an API's documentation to find the correct endpoint for what you actually need is the first real step in using any new API.

contentSections.body: Many public APIs are free to use for small, personal projects, sometimes with a rate limit (a cap on how many requests you can make per minute or day) and sometimes requiring a free API key just to identify who's asking (more on keys in lesson 5). The API's documentation — a page, usually, listing every endpoint and exactly what each one expects and returns — is the actual source of truth for what's available; guessing at endpoint URLs is not a reliable substitute for reading it.
An endpoint is one specific URL for one specific question. The wrong endpoint returns real, valid data — just not the data you meant to ask for.

description: fetch() sends the actual network request — but what comes back isn't your data yet, it's a wrapper around it, and getting the real, usable data out takes one more explicit step.

learningObjectives.text: Send a request to a URL with fetch()
Explain that fetch's response is a wrapper object, not the data itself
Extract usable data from a response with .json()

contentSections.title: fetch() sends the request

contentSections.body: You've found the right endpoint for today's weather. Now you actually need to send that request over the network — and JavaScript has one built-in function whose whole job is exactly that.

contentSections.scenario: You want to request data from 'https://api.example.com/current?city=Boston'.
contentSections.question: Which line actually sends that request?

options.label: fetch('https://api.example.com/current?city=Boston')
request('https://api.example.com/current?city=Boston')
fetch(https://api.example.com/current?city=Boston)

feedback.correct: Right. fetch(url) is the built-in browser function for sending a network request to a given URL, with the URL passed as a quoted string.
feedback.wrong_name: There's no built-in function called request — the actual built-in name is fetch, and it's the one every browser provides for this.
feedback.no_quotes: Without quotes, JavaScript tries to read this as an actual expression (dividing values, essentially), not as the URL text — a URL, like any specific piece of text, needs to be a quoted string.

contentSections.concept: fetch(url) sends a network request to the given URL — the browser's built-in tool for exactly this. Just calling fetch() starts the request in motion; what it actually gives back needs one more step to turn into usable data, which is what the rest of this lesson covers.

contentSections.body: fetch(url) sends the request. What comes back needs one more step before it's usable data — covered next.

contentSections.title: The response isn't your data yet — it's a wrapper around it

contentSections.body: You log the response straight to the console, expecting to see today's temperature. Instead you get a strange object labeled "Response," with properties like status and headers, and nothing that looks like actual weather data anywhere in it.

contentSections.question: response.temperature is undefined, even though the API genuinely does return temperature data. What's actually wrong?

options.label: response is a wrapper object (status, headers, and a body that hasn't been read yet) — the real data has to be extracted from it, not read directly off it
The API doesn't actually return temperature data
temperature is misspelled somewhere in the actual API

feedback.wrapper: Right. The response object is a wrapper carrying metadata about the request (did it succeed, what status code, what headers) plus an unread body — the actual JSON data is inside that body, and has to be explicitly extracted.
feedback.no_data: The API does return real temperature data — it's just not sitting as a direct property on the response wrapper object, which is a separate, generic object regardless of what specific data any given API returns.
feedback.spelling: This isn't a spelling issue in the request — the real property name doesn't matter yet, because nothing has extracted the actual JSON body from the response wrapper at all.

contentSections.body: This two-step shape — get the response wrapper, then call `.json()` on it to get the real data — is standard for every fetch call returning JSON, not specific to any one API. The response wrapper also carries useful metadata beyond the body, like `response.status` (the HTTP status code) and `response.ok` (a quick true/false for "did this succeed") — both of which matter a lot once lesson 4 covers what happens when a request fails.
fetch's response is a wrapper, not the data itself. .json() extracts and parses the real body — and itself needs its own .then().

title: Waiting: async code, gently
description: The network doesn't answer instantly, and JavaScript doesn't pause and wait for it by default — async/await is how you tell specific code to actually wait for a result before moving on.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why code run immediately after fetch() sees undefined instead of the response
Use await inside an async function to pause until a fetch resolves
Explain why await only works inside a function marked async

contentSections.title: The network doesn't answer instantly

contentSections.body: You write `const response = fetch(url); console.log(response);` expecting to see the response object. Instead you get something that isn't the data at all — because the network request takes real time, and JavaScript didn't wait around for it before running the very next line.

contentSections.question: Why does this log something other than the real response data, right away?

options.label: fetch doesn't pause the program to wait for the network — it immediately returns a Promise, a placeholder for a value that will show up later
The URL is invalid
console.log can't display network responses

feedback.promise: Right. fetch() returns immediately with a Promise — a real value representing "data that isn't ready yet, but will be" — rather than freezing the whole program until the actual network round trip finishes.
feedback.invalid_url: This isn't about whether the URL works — the exact same thing happens with a perfectly valid, working URL, because it's about timing, not correctness.
feedback.cant_log: console.log can display a Promise object just fine — it's genuinely what's there at that exact moment, before the network request has had time to complete.

contentSections.mechanism: A network request takes real, unpredictable time — milliseconds to seconds — and JavaScript doesn't stop everything else to wait for it. Instead, fetch() immediately hands back a **Promise**: a placeholder object representing "a value that will exist eventually." Code written directly after a fetch call, on the very next line, runs before that promise has resolved into real data — which is exactly why logging it immediately shows a Promise, not the data itself.

contentSections.body: fetch() returns immediately with a Promise, not the real data — await is what actually pauses until that data is ready.

contentSections.title: await only works inside an async function

contentSections.body: You try dropping `await fetch(url)` directly into your regular top-level code, the way you'd write any other line — and instead of pausing correctly, it throws a syntax error before the page even runs.

contentSections.question: This throws a syntax error immediately. What's actually missing?

options.label: await is being used outside an async function — it only works inside a function specifically marked async
fetch is spelled wrong
The URL needs to be wrapped in extra parentheses

feedback.not_async: Right. await is only valid syntax inside a function declared with the async keyword — using it at the top level (outside any async function) throws a syntax error in most environments.
feedback.spelling: fetch is spelled correctly here — this isn't a naming issue at all, it's about where await is allowed to appear.
feedback.parens: Extra parentheses around the URL wouldn't fix anything — the actual problem is structural, about which kind of function this code is running inside.

contentSections.body: A useful mental shortcut: any function containing `await` has to be declared `async function functionName() { ... }`. Calling that async function doesn't block the rest of the page either — everything outside it keeps running normally while the async function itself waits internally at each `await`, which is what keeps the page responsive instead of freezing during a slow network request.
await is only legal inside a function marked async — the two keywords are a matched pair.

title: When the request fails, and what the user sees
description: A network request can fail outright, or come back with a real HTTP error status the browser doesn't treat as a failure by default — both need to be handled deliberately, or the page just quietly does nothing.

learningObjectives.text: Wrap an await fetch in try/catch to handle real network failures
Explain that fetch does not reject on HTTP error statuses like 404 by default
Check response.ok explicitly to catch HTTP-level failures

contentSections.title: The network doesn't always work

contentSections.body: Someone's checking your symptom-tracking page from their phone in bed, and the WiFi drops mid-request — extremely common, not an edge case, for exactly the audience this track is built for. With no handling for that, the page doesn't show an error. It just... does nothing, forever, with no explanation.

contentSections.scenario: Two ways a page might behave when a fetch request genuinely fails (no network connection at all).
contentSections.question: Which is the better experience for whoever's using the page?

options.label: A visible message: "Couldn't load weather data — check your connection and try again"
A loading spinner that never resolves, with no explanation of what's wrong
A completely blank section, with nothing at all indicating anything happened

feedback.clear_message: Right. A specific, honest message tells someone exactly what happened and what they can try — the actual goal of handling a failure well, not just technically catching it.
feedback.stuck_spinner: A spinner that never resolves actively lies about the situation — it implies something is still in progress, when the truth is the request has already failed and nothing further is coming.
feedback.blank: A blank section with zero explanation leaves someone unable to tell the difference between "there's genuinely nothing here" and "something broke" — no useful information either way.

contentSections.concept: A failed request needs to be caught and turned into a real, honest message — not left to produce a frozen spinner or a silent blank page. This is exactly the same principle from the storing-data module's corrupted-save handling, applied to network requests instead of localStorage: a real failure, handled deliberately, beats a silent one.

contentSections.body: A real network failure needs try/catch and a genuine, honest message — not a spinner that never resolves or a silent blank page.

contentSections.title: fetch doesn't throw just because the server said "not found"

contentSections.body: You request an endpoint with a typo in the URL, and the server correctly responds "404, not found." Your try/catch — which you were sure would handle exactly this — doesn't fire at all. The code inside try runs all the way through as if nothing went wrong.

contentSections.question: The URL is wrong and the server returns a real 404 error status — but catch never fires. Why?

options.label: fetch only rejects (triggering catch) on genuine network failures — it does NOT reject just because the server responded with an HTTP error status like 404
404 errors are automatically retried until they succeed
try/catch doesn't work with async functions

feedback.no_reject_on_status: Right. From fetch's point of view, receiving a real, well-formed "404, not found" response is a successful round trip — a genuine response did come back, it just happens to describe an error, which fetch doesn't treat as a rejection on its own.
feedback.auto_retry: There's no automatic retry behavior here — the request runs once, gets its one response, and that's the end of it.
feedback.no_try_catch_async: try/catch works completely normally with async/await — the reason catch didn't fire isn't a syntax limitation, it's that nothing here actually threw.

contentSections.mechanism: fetch() only rejects (which is what triggers `catch`) for genuine network-level failures — no connection, a DNS failure, a timeout. An HTTP error status like 404 (not found) or 500 (server error) still counts as a completed, successful round trip as far as fetch is concerned; the server answered, it just answered with bad news. Catching that requires explicitly checking `response.ok` (a boolean, true only for successful status codes) or `response.status` after the fetch, not relying on try/catch alone.

contentSections.body: try/catch handles a request that never completes. response.ok handles a request that completes but reports an error — you need both.

title: Keys, secrets and what never goes in a web page
description: Any JavaScript shipped to a browser is fully readable by anyone who opens the page's source — an API key pasted directly into that code is effectively public the moment the page is, no matter how carefully it's hidden in the file.

learningObjectives.text: Explain that all client-side JavaScript is fully visible to anyone viewing the page
Judge that an API key hardcoded in frontend JavaScript is effectively exposed to the public
Identify a server-side proxy as the real fix for keeping a key secret, as a concept to revisit later

contentSections.title: An API key is a password for the API

contentSections.body: You sign up for a weather API and get a personal API key — a long string that identifies you as the one making requests, used for tracking usage and sometimes billing. The most direct way to use it seems obvious: paste it right into your JavaScript, exactly where fetch() needs it. That direct approach is also the one that publishes it to literally anyone who visits your page.

contentSections.scenario: A developer hardcodes their weather API key directly into their page's JavaScript file, which is then deployed live on the internet.
contentSections.question: Which of these are true about that key, once the page is live?

items.label: Anyone can see the key by opening the browser's "view page source" or developer tools
Anyone who copies the key can use it in their own requests, under the original developer's account
Minifying or obfuscating the JavaScript makes the key genuinely secret
The key is safe as long as it isn't linked from the page's visible navigation

explanation.view_source: True, and this is the core of the whole problem — every byte of JavaScript sent to a browser is downloaded to that browser and fully readable, by design, regardless of how it's formatted or where in the file it sits.
explanation.usable_by_others: True — a copied key generally works exactly as well for anyone else as it does for the original account holder, since the API has no way to tell who's actually using it beyond the key itself.
explanation.minified_hidden: False — minifying (compressing variable names, removing whitespace) makes code harder for a human to casually read, but it's still fully downloaded and can be trivially reformatted back into readable text. It's an obstacle of seconds, not real protection.
explanation.safe_if_unlinked: False — the key isn't protected by not being linked anywhere; it's sitting directly in a JavaScript file that's downloaded to every single visitor's browser the moment they load the page, discoverable, unlinked or not.

contentSections.synthesis: There's no version of "hide it better within the frontend code" that actually works — anything running in a browser is downloaded, in full, to that browser. The problem isn't how carefully the key is placed; it's that frontend JavaScript was never a place capable of keeping anything secret.

contentSections.body: This matters beyond "someone might use my free quota" — for a paid API, an exposed key can mean real, unexpected charges run up by strangers. Even for a free API, a leaked key can get rate-limited or banned entirely because of someone else's usage, breaking your own app in the process.
Everything in a browser's JavaScript is fully downloaded and readable by anyone — there's no way to genuinely hide a secret inside frontend code.

contentSections.title: So where does the key actually go?

contentSections.body: If the key can't live in the browser at all, and the page still needs the data that key unlocks — where does it actually go? This track hasn't built a real server yet, so the honest, short answer previews something a later module covers properly.

contentSections.question: A free weather API's terms say the worst case for an exposed key is "your free daily request quota might run out faster." A different, paid API's key is directly tied to a credit card being charged per request. Is hardcoding the key into frontend JavaScript an equally bad idea for both?
contentSections.hint: The underlying exposure (anyone can read and reuse the key) is identical in both cases — what differs is the actual cost of that exposure.
contentSections.answer: The exposure itself is identical either way — the key is equally readable and equally reusable by a stranger in both cases. What differs is the consequence: a burned-through free quota is annoying but bounded; unexpected charges on a paid, per-request API are a genuinely serious, open-ended problem. The lesson isn't "never hardcode a key, ever, under any circumstances" — it's understanding exactly what's at risk before deciding a shortcut is acceptable, rather than assuming it's fine by default.

contentSections.body: The real fix is a **server-side proxy**: instead of the browser calling the API directly with the key attached, the browser calls *your own* small server, which holds the key privately (never sent to any browser) and makes the actual API request on the page's behalf, then passes just the resulting data back. The key never leaves a place only you control. This requires an actual backend — the "When You Need a Backend" module, later in this track, covers building exactly that server piece properly. For now, in a learning project with no real secret at stake, using a key directly in frontend code for a free, low-risk API is a reasonable shortcut — the rule to actually carry forward is knowing the difference between that shortcut and something that would be a real problem if exposed, and not treating the shortcut as the permanent answer once real stakes are involved.
A real fix keeps the key on a server you control, never sent to the browser at all — a later module builds exactly that. Until then, know what's actually at risk before taking the shortcut.

title: Practice — Handle Seven API Responses, Including Failures
description: Seven drills, no new concepts: given a fetch scenario — successful, slow, failed, or reporting an HTTP error — diagnose or write the code that handles it correctly.

learningObjectives.text: Apply fetch, async/await, try/catch and response.ok checks to small stated API scenarios

contentSections.title: Seven responses, the same handful of rules

contentSections.body: Every one of these traces back to something from this module: fetch returns a Promise you have to await, .json() unwraps the real body, try/catch handles a request that never completes, and response.ok handles one that completes with bad news.
Almost every fetch bug in this module comes down to one question: am I waiting for this correctly, and have I handled both ways it can fail?

title: Lab — Build a Page Powered by a Public API
description: A real page, showing real data from a real public API — with every state this module has been teaching you to handle: loading, empty, and error, not just the happy path where everything works.

learningObjectives.text: Fetch real data from a public API and display it on a page
Show a genuine loading state while a request is in flight
Handle both network failures and HTTP error responses with real, visible feedback

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Pick a genuinely free, no-signup-required public API (a weather API, a quotes API, a public data API of some kind) and build a small page around it — one that behaves correctly not just when everything goes right, but while it's waiting, when there's nothing to show, and when something breaks.

contentSections.title: Build a page powered by a public API
contentSections.brief: Choose a free public API that needs no signup or key (or one with a generous free tier where a key is safe to use directly, per lesson 5's judgment). Build a page that fetches real data from it and displays it, handling the request's full lifecycle — not just the successful case.
contentSections.deliverable: A working page with loading, empty and error states all handled.

stages.title: The happy path, including an empty result
stages.instructions: Write an async function that awaits fetch(url), checks response.ok, awaits response.json(), and displays real data from the response on the page using textContent (not innerHTML, per the JavaScript module's rule). Also check whether the parsed data could ever come back empty (an empty list of results, for instance) — if so, show a clear "No data found" message in that case instead of a blank, unexplained gap.
stages.checkpoint: Real data from the chosen API is correctly fetched and displayed, and a genuinely empty result shows an explicit message rather than a blank area.

stages.title: A real loading state
stages.instructions: Show a visible "Loading..." message (or similar) the moment the fetch starts, and remove it once real data is displayed (or once an error state takes over). The loading indicator should never be left showing forever, even in a failure case — check this by simulating a slow connection if your browser's dev tools allow it, or by deliberately breaking the URL temporarily.
stages.checkpoint: A loading indicator appears while the request is in flight and is reliably removed once it resolves, one way or another.

stages.title: A real network failure
stages.instructions: Wrap the fetch in try/catch. Temporarily break the URL (a typo in the domain, not just the path) to simulate a real network failure, confirm the catch block fires and displays a genuine, readable message — not a console-only log — then fix the URL back.
stages.checkpoint: A deliberately broken URL produces a real, visible error message on the page, not a silent failure or a stuck loading state.

stages.title: A real HTTP error response
stages.instructions: Temporarily change the URL to a valid domain but a wrong path (something likely to return a real 404 from the same API), confirm your response.ok check catches it and shows an honest message distinct from the network-failure case, then fix the URL back to the correct endpoint.
stages.checkpoint: A request that completes with an HTTP error status is caught by a response.ok check and shown with its own honest message.

rubric.criterion: Real data loads and displays correctly, empty results included
rubric.meets: The happy path fetches real data and displays it using textContent, and a genuinely empty result shows an explicit "No data found" message rather than a blank gap.

rubric.criterion: A loading state is shown and reliably cleared
rubric.meets: A visible loading indicator appears during the request and disappears in every outcome — success, network failure, or HTTP error.

rubric.criterion: A genuine network failure is handled with a real message
rubric.meets: try/catch is present, and a simulated network failure produces a visible, honest message rather than a silent or stuck page.

rubric.criterion: An HTTP error response is handled separately from a network failure
rubric.meets: response.ok is checked explicitly, and a simulated HTTP error (like a 404) shows its own distinct message.

rubric.criterion: No secret is exposed carelessly
rubric.meets: If the chosen API needs a key, its exposure risk was consciously weighed per lesson 5, not just pasted in without thought.

contentSections.body: A page that only works when the network cooperates isn't done — the loading, empty and error states are exactly the states real, unreliable networks will actually put someone in.

A Promise — a placeholder for data that will exist eventually
undefined, with no further information

questions.explanation: fetch() doesn't pause the program to wait — it immediately returns a Promise, and await is what actually pauses until that Promise resolves into real data.

questions.from: This module — Getting Data From Elsewhere
questions.prompt: Why does a fetch request to a URL that returns a real HTTP 404 not get caught by try/catch on its own?

options.label: fetch only rejects on genuine network failures — a completed response, even an error one like 404, isn't treated as a rejection
try/catch doesn't work with async functions
404 errors are automatically retried, so the catch never has a reason to fire

questions.explanation: A 404 is still a genuine, completed round trip from fetch's point of view — the server answered, just with bad news. Catching it needs an explicit response.ok check, not just try/catch.

questions.from: This module — Getting Data From Elsewhere
questions.prompt: What does the async keyword on a function actually enable?

options.label: It makes the function run faster
It allows await to be used legally inside that function's body
It automatically retries failed requests

questions.explanation: await is only valid syntax inside a function declared async — the two keywords are a matched pair, and async doesn't change execution speed on its own.

options.label: All JavaScript sent to a browser is fully downloaded and readable by anyone, regardless of formatting — the key is effectively public
Minified code is technically invalid and will fail to run
There's no real risk as long as the key isn't linked in the page's navigation

options.label: A string
Whatever type was originally saved
A boolean

options.label: The default string conversion discards the object's actual properties — JSON.stringify is needed to preserve them
Objects can never be saved to localStorage under any circumstances
This only happens on certain browsers

questions.explanation: localStorage's generic conversion of an object produces the unhelpful "[object Object]" text. JSON.stringify converts it into a real, data-preserving JSON string instead.

options.label: null
An empty string
It throws an error

try/catch is required syntax for JSON.parse to run at all
JSON.parse always throws on the first call

questions.explanation: 4.5:1 for normal text — a real, checkable minimum, not a matter of visual taste.

One long list of plain numbers
A single record with one field per entry
